articles.title: Japan’s empty temples seek new ways to survive
articles.summary: The 370-year-old structure has all the attributes of a classically designed Japanese temple, from the curved roof to the timber-frame walls, spacious tatami-mat prayer hall and elaborately decorated…

blocks.text: The 370-year-old structure has all the attributes of a classically designed Japanese temple, from the curved roof to the timber-frame walls, spacious tatami-mat prayer hall and elaborately decorated altar.

Set in manicured gardens on the Chita Peninsula in central Japan, the 350-square-meter (3,767-square-foot) property is on the market for 482 million yen (€2.66 million, US3.01 million). The estate agent’s pitch says the price includes dismantling by “expert heritage craftsmen” and delivery to anywhere in Japan, where it would be fully restored into a “stunning” two- or three-bedroom home.
The sale and removal of the temple marks the end of its role in the local community in the hills above the Nagasawacho district, but it is a better fate than many places of worship across Japan.

There are around 77,000 temples across the country, but as many as 17,000 no longer have a full-time resident priest as congregations have shrunk — particularly in rural districts experiencing rapid depopulation — and financial pressures have taken their toll.
That means many temples are being sold off or simply shuttered and left to deteriorate quietly.
A temple brought back to life
Tomomi Iwayama took on the abandoned Ganshu-ji temple in Odawara, a coastal town about 80 kilometers (50 miles) southwest of Tokyo, a decade ago. Today, he is the abbot of a growing congregation.
“The temple had no abbot for 70 years before I arrived because it was just so difficult to operate, and it has taken me until now to get it financially back on track,” he told DW.
“Even in a relatively large urban area such as Odawara, which has around 200,000 residents, it has been very hard,” he said. “In the countryside, it is much more difficult.”

Iwayama’s biggest problem is the country’s shrinking population: fewer worshippers and falling demand for funerals and other traditional rites make it harder to finance the temple’s upkeep. He has worked hard to reach out to the local community and has had success in selling plots in the temple graveyard.
One innovation that has attracted attention is the temple’s “smart graveyard,” where families scan a card, and a robotic system recovers a relative’s ashes from the columbarium.
Temples in rural areas of Japan face far greater challenges, he said.

“Young people in villages usually leave to go to university, and then they find a job in one of the big cities, so they rarely go back,” he said. “Maybe they will go back once a year to pay their respects to their ancestors at the village temple, but that is not enough for the temple to get by on.”

Equally, when the head priest of a rural temple retires, his children are unlikely to want to take the role on because of these challenges. All too often, Iwayama said, the result is the temple closing.
But he denies the suggestion that religion in Japan is following the same path as in the West, where Christian congregation numbers have plummeted over the decades.
Demand for Buddhism remains
“I sense there is still a lot of demand in Japan for Buddhism,” he said, contrasting the fast-paced, technology-focused lives that people typically lead with the serenity that they are often seeking.

“Buddhism is a style of living, of an enlightened person,” he said. “A lot of people are looking for that. And while the traditional rituals of funerals and anniversaries are declining and that revenue is shrinking, we are finding that more people want to take part in traditional temple cuisine cooking classes, meditation and other things that we can offer.”
Temples that are not able to shift to offer experiences more in tune with modern Japan are at risk of closing, said Joey Stockermans, one of the founders of the Mokomoko online real estate service.
“We have had a temple on our site in the past, and we were approached by a foreign potential buyer, so there is certainly interest when these properties become available,” he said.

Other foreigners who are long-term residents are doing their best to protect Japan’s religious heritage for future generations. American journalist and author Jake Adelstein is currently a Zen priest at Zenshoin Temple in Tokyo’s Toshima Ward and is training to become an abbot.

“I do not think that Japanese are becoming less religious; I believe they are becoming fewer because of population decline, and they are becoming less wealthy because of the economic situation,” he said.

“Families want to keep the grave plot that they have had for generations, but for many of them it is just too expensive to maintain, and they often live a long way away, so they are unable to regularly visit to pay their respects,” he said.
The annual fee for a grave can be up to 100,000 yen, while memorials and other rites can be an additional financial burden, Adelstein explained.
Young people shun religious careers

“Young people are not interested in a career as a priest because temples earn so little money, so there are positions that cannot be filled, and that is especially a problem in the countryside,” he said.
Some temples have amalgamated their operations and share a priest, but that will become more difficult in the future, Adelstein said.
As elsewhere, Zenshoin Temple has started vegetarian cooking classes and Zen meditation sessions to appeal to the local community, and Adelstein hopes that will be enough to keep the temple open.
“The training to become an abbot is very tough, and the economics of a temple today often just do not add up, but I see it as a critical part of this society and this nation,” he said. /dl

articles.title: Tens of millions of people fail to get humanitarian aid as global system crumbles
articles.summary:
Funding cuts in 2025 left women, children, older and displaced people hard hit, with 64m fewer people receiving aid

The humanitarian aid system is crumbling as funding shrinks, pressures…

blocks.text: The humanitarian aid system is crumbling as funding shrinks, pressures increase and governments not only fail to protect civilians but are increasingly responsible for endangering them, a new report warned on Thursday as figures revealed 64 million fewer people received aid last year.

With aid contributions cut by 30% between 2022 and 2025 and thousands of aid workers losing their jobs, the humanitarian system has suffered one of its biggest contractions since being formed in the post-second world war era, according to the State of the Humanitarian System 2026 report.
In 2025, only those whose lives were in immediate danger became the focus, while support for longer-term issues and the ability to recover from crises was drastically scaled back.

Jennifer Doherty, co-author of the report produced by the humanitarian organisation Active Learning Network for Accountability and Performance (Alnap), said: “The impacts were not felt equally. The combination of reduced funding and restrictive politics meant women, children, elderly people and displaced people were especially hardest hit.”
Doherty, who said up to 23% of humanitarian staffing was estimated to have been lost in 2025, said: “Specialised services closed and targeted support became harder to sustain.”
According to the report, funding fell to an estimated $33.3bn (£24.6bn) in 2025, from a peak of $47.5bn in 2022.
While USAID sustained the most dramatic cuts, with a 55% reduction in 2025, there were also cuts by other leading donors, with 13 of the top 20 reducing their aid donations last year.

The report also highlighted the growing pressure from governments on how aid could be spent, such as the US spending freeze on programmes considered driven by diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.

The aid cuts also meant that for the few people who did receive support, the targeted amount for each person dropped from $178 in 2021 to $90 in 2025, despite the actual needs of each person having risen to $255.

An aggravating factor was that governments not only failed in their duties to protect civilians but were also often actually endangering people. States were responsible for 64% of attacks on healthcare workers and largely responsible for violence that affected aid workers through the use of airstrikes.

blocks.caption: Displaced people receive food aid in Al-Khawkhah, in Yemen’s Hodeidah province, in July. Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Yemen was one of the countries badly affected by aid cuts, with nutrition worsening and diphtheria cases rising because vaccination campaigns were suspended.
Mohammed Bahashwan, Action for Humanity’s country director in Yemen, said diminishing levels of aid were exacerbating the crises faced by families.

“Problems are not occurring separately. A family may have lost its income, be unable to afford food, have a malnourished child and still need to travel considerable distances or pay costs they cannot afford to access healthcare,” he said.

The report said there were examples of the humanitarian system mobilising to support those most in need, often led by local aid organisations, and of diaspora networks stepping in. But it also said the international system did not coordinate well with these networks and that it was often local aid organisations and staff who were worst affected by cuts.

Meg Sattler, chief executive of the Vienna-based organisation Ground Truth Solutions, which carries out regular surveys of people who need aid, said there should be more focus on localisation because the international humanitarian system had not adapted fast enough or pushed back against the cuts and stipulations imposed by the US.

“We have definitely spoken to people feeling the pinch of this contraction. It is especially causing distress where aid is now considered ‘life-saving only’ and isn’t letting people do things such as send their kids to school or save to start a business – things that would help them be less reliant on aid in the future,” she said.

articles.title: Climate ‘feedback loops’ could worsen global warming by 30%, study finds
articles.summary:
Emissions of planet-heating methane and CO2 from natural sources are worsening the climate crisis, paper says

Rising global temperatures caused by the burning of fossil fuels are…

blocks.text: Rising global temperatures caused by the burning of fossil fuels are transforming the world’s forests, wetlands and tundra to the point they are releasing emissions that could further worsen global heating by as much as 30%, a new study has found.

As the world heats up, permafrost in the high latitudes is thawing, fiercer wildfires are burning in drying forests and wetlands and lakes are warming. All of these changes are themselves causing the release of planet-heating methane and carbon dioxide locked in trees and soils, therefore worsening the climate crisis, the paper states.

While scientists have long known of these “feedback loops” that amplify the impact of direct pollution from burning coal, oil and gas, the emissions from natural sources are largely unaccounted for in climate projections.

This additional heating is however significant, researchers found, with emissions from natural sources set to amplify global heating by 20% to 30% by the end of this century. This would add an estimated 0.2C to 0.4C to the global average temperature by this time, depending on the overall action taken by countries to combat the climate crisis.

blocks.caption: Fumaroles are seen in an area of cultivated cattail swamps to mitigate air pollution threat at the Salton Sea on 19 February 2021 near Calipatria, California.   Photograph: David McNew/Getty Images

blocks.text: Even small fractions of temperature change across the global climate can greatly change the risk of severe and deadly heatwaves, floods, drought and other impacts.

The United Nations last week conceded the international pact to constraint the global temperature rise to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels will be breached in the next few years, causing climate impacts such as this summer’s record heatwaves and wildfires to “strike faster, hit harder and last longer.”

Yet the increase in the world’s fever will likely be even larger than most projections currently account for, the new research warns, as they do not factor in the methane and CO2 that will spew from permafrost, wetlands, freshwaters and wildfires – the four areas the paper analyzed.

“This hidden multiplier is missing from the models guiding climate policy, so those models are likely underestimating how much warming is coming – and overestimating how much carbon we can still afford to emit,” said Sam Abernethy, a scientist at Spark Climate Solutions Research who led the research, published in Environmental Research Letters.

The disruption of the world’s carbon cycles is now being seen in “real time”, said Rob Jackson, a Stanford University scientist and study co-author. “The results are a wake-up call, and it’s imperative that they be included in the next generation of climate policies,” he added. “Failure to do so will make meeting the world’s climate goals less and less likely.”

There has been long-standing concern that should global heating melt enough of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, thaw enough permafrost, warp crucial ocean currents and turn the Amazon rainforest into a savannah, the world will career past a series of catastrophic tipping points where the climate system spins wildly outside any sort of restraining human influence.
The planet is getting closer to such a “point of no return” where this runaway global heating becomes reality, a separate study earlier this year warned.

blocks.caption: Severe erosion of the permafrost tundra in the Yukon Delta, Alaska in 2019. According to scientists emissions from natural sources set to amplify global heating by 20% to 30% by the end of this century. Photograph: Mark Ralston/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: This latest paper makes clear that action by countries to cut fossil fuel pollution will still lessen the amount of additional emissions that come from landscapes. Under the most optimistic climate scenario where emissions are cut quickly, natural sources will add 0.2C of warming, the paper found. Under a worse case higher emissions scenario, 0.4C will likely be added.

Current policies put in place by governments are likely to see the global temperature rise to 2.6C above pre-industrial times, according to Climate Action Tracker. This will likely cause severe disruption and hardship to billions of people through sea level rise, crop losses and other consequences.

“One of the most troubling aspects of climate change is that warming can trigger natural processes that cause still more warming,” said Bill Ripple, an ecologist at Oregon State University who helped author the research earlier this year on runaway heating. He was not involved in the new paper, which he called “important”.

“This does not mean that a Hothouse Earth trajectory is inevitable, but it provides another warning about the possibility of reinforcing feedbacks that can amplify the warming humans initiate,” he said.

“The paper also reminds us why every fraction of a degree matters. The more we warm the planet, the more we risk activating natural processes that add still more greenhouse gases to the atmosphere. This makes rapid reductions in fossil fuel emissions even more urgent.”

articles.title: Dy dynasty dominates Isabela for decades
articles.summary: Through strong and longstanding alliances, the Dy clan continues its dominance over Isabela politics, securing national and local posts mostly unopposed

blocks.text: Editor’s note: This is part of a Rappler series on Filipino families that have held political power for generations. The series traces how they built their influence, where it is strongest, and how it has endured over time. Each profile examines family ties, political networks, business interests, and roles in local and national government.
When Faustino “Bojie” Dy III assumed the speakership of the House of Representatives, the national spotlight shone on him — and on the deep political roots of his family back home.
The Dy dynasty’s rule over Isabela province began with patriarch Faustino Dy Sr. in the 1960s. He started his political career as a local councilor before becoming the mayor of Cauayan.

By 1971, the clan’s hold on the provincial capitol was established when he was elected governor for the first time. He occupied the top seat for 18 years, with a brief gap term in between, making him the longest-serving governor of Isabela to date.
The power was later passed down to his sons. Benjamin Dy served as governor from 1992 to 2001, followed by Faustino Dy Jr. from 2001 to 2004.
Another son, Faustino “Bojie” Dy III, stepped into the governorship in 2010, holding the post until reaching his term limit in 2019.

Rather than exiting the capitol, Bojie slid down to vice governor in the 2019 elections. He served until 2025 before taking over the seat of his son, Faustino “Inno” Dy V, as the representative of Isabela’s 6th District.
Currently, the Dy political dynasty simultaneously holds nine key positions across local and national fronts, according to the Congressional Policy and Budget Research Department.
A timeline mapping the notable rotation and overlap of local government positions held by the Dy family across three decades.
Scroll or swipe right to see the dynasty’s full timeline. Tap or hover a bar for details, including family ties and each member’s years in power.
Source: Comelec, public records

At the national level, Bojie Dy leads as House Speaker, anchoring a three-member family bloc in the 20th Congress that commands half of the province’s six legislative districts. Joining him are his nephews Faustino Michael Carlos “Mike” Dy III and Ian Paul Dy, representing Isabela’s 5th and 3rd District, respectively.

In the local scene, the dynasty maintains a multi-generational grip on provincial and municipal seats. In the provincial government, Bojie’s son Francis Faustino “Kiko” Dy, a former Echague mayor, serves as vice governor, while Bojie’s nephew, Manuel Faustino “King” Dy, sits on the provincial board.
Across Isabela’s towns, four other family members head key local executive and legislative offices:

items: Faustino “Inno” Dy V (son of Bojie, former 6th district representative) serves as mayor of Echague
Faustino “Dondon” Dy IV (son of Bojie) serves as the mayor of San Manuel
Caesar “Jaycee” Dy Jr. (nephew of Bojie) serves as the mayor of Cauayan City
Benjamin “Benjie” Dy III (nephew of Bojie) serves as the vice mayor of Cauayan City

blocks.text: This broad consolidation of authority was built on strategic alignments first forged by their patriarch Faustino Dy Sr., who closely aligned himself with the late dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos during and after the Martial Law years.
This historical Dy-Marcos alignment endures today, with Bojie now steering the clan’s national ties.
In the 2022 presidential elections, Bojie endorsed now-President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., helping deliver a decisive landslide victory across Isabela against the latter’s political rivals.

blocks.caption: FAMILY. Bojie Dy and his family attend the swearing-in ceremony of his son, Echague Mayor Faustino ‘Inno’ Dy V. Photo from Inno’s FB Page

blocks.text: Beyond national ties, the Dys have also fortified their reign through their pacts with other local political powerhouses in their home province.

The Dy dynasty is closely tied to the Albano clan. The two families have been jointly governing Isabela for decades, maintaining continuous control and frequently rotating roles in major provincial and congressional seats.

While the Dys have kept the governorship to themselves for decades, term-limited Bojie’s transition to vice governor in 2019 allowed the Albanos to take the helm at the capitol. Since then, a Dy has yet to return to the provincial government’s top seat.
Yet far from marking a decline in influence, this strategic co-governance has only cemented the dual dominance of both families over Isabela’s political landscape.
Another political powerhouse firmly within the Dy network is the Tan clan of Santiago City.
In 2021, Bojie’s son, Inno Dy, married Alyssa Sheena Tan, who currently leads Santiago City as mayor.
Through this alliance, the Dys extended their influence in Congress through Sheena’s brother, Joseph Tan, who represents Isabela’s 4th District.

blocks.caption: MEETING. Isabela politicians, including members of the Dy family, meet with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Photo from Faustino Michael Carlos T. Dy III’s Facebook page.

blocks.text: With formidable backing from both local and national allies, challenging the Dys has proven to be a near-impossible task. Their electoral track record remains almost spotless, recording successive victories at the polls.

The Dys’ monopoly over the provincial capitol was cracked only twice in recent history, when former broadcast journalist and Ramon Magsaysay Awardee Grace Padaca snapped the clan’s long-ruling leadership in the 2004 and 2007 gubernatorial races.

Padaca’s political trajectory began in 2001 with a controversial run against Bojie Dy for Isabela’s 3rd District congressional seat. After initially trailing by 1,285 votes, Padaca contested the results before the House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal (HRET), citing alleged dagdag-bawas (vote-padding and shaving) operations in the municipality of Angadanan.
Following a lengthy process, the tribunal ultimately ruled in favor of Dy by a razor-thin margin of just 48 votes, largely after invalidating ballots simply marked as “Grace”.
Padaca redeemed herself in the 2004 elections by defeating then-incumbent governor Faustino Dy Jr., officially snapping the family’s governorship streak.
In a 2004 interview, she said that public outrage over alleged manipulation in 2001 and a growing desire to “free themselves from the claws of a dynasty” were critical factors in her victory.
She went on to secure a second term in 2007 against Benjamin Dy.
Her victories, however, proved to be a temporary pause rather than an end to the dynasty’s reign.
Padaca’s bid for a third term in 2010 was thwarted when Bojie Dy reclaimed the governorship for the family.
She mounted another challenge in 2019 by running for vice governor, initially aligning with Napoleon “Pol” Dy, who had a rift with his brother, then-governor Bojie.
But when the brothers reconciled, Pol withdrew his gubernatorial bid, leaving Padaca without a running mate. She ultimately lost the race to Bojie Dy.
Since then, the Dy clan’s grip has only tightened, developing into a multi-generational takeover of the country’s second-largest province.
In recent elections, their candidates faced virtually no opposition in key races, with Bojie, Ian Paul, and Mike sweeping congressional seats while Kiko secured the vice governorship.

Strategic alliances are only part of the equation behind the Dys’ enduring dominance. According to a social science instructor at a local Isabela university, “dyadic clientelism” plays a central role in how voters engage with the clan.

“Iyong mga politicians, they provide ayuda, goods, and services na need ng mga tao. Dahil dito mas nagiging reliant [sila] sa concept ng patronage system sa Pilipinas,” the instructor said, referencing Julio G. Teehankee’s Patronage Democracy in the Philippines: Clans, Clients, and Competition in Local Elections.
(Politicians provide aid, goods, and services that people need. Because of this, [people] become more reliant on the concept of the patronage system in the Philippines.)

“Halimbawa na lang iyong scholarship na nakapangalan sa kanila. Tinatawag kasi itong BRO-Ed Scholarship. Branding kumbaga. (Take for instance the scholarship program carrying their name. It’s called the BRO-Ed Scholarship. It is a matter of branding.)”
“BRO-Ed” stands for Bojie-Rodito Opportunities for Education, named after House Speaker Bojie Dy and Governor Rodolfo “Rodito” Albano III, a direct reflection of their political partnership.
During the 2022 elections, The LaSallian reported that local program coordinators allegedly pressured Isabela government scholars to support the Marcos Jr.-Duterte campaign.
The Isabela Provincial Scholarship Program, said in a statement that the post was a “mere invitation” with no intention of coercing student-scholars.
With extensive political machinery and public resources at their disposal, the instructor emphasized that the Dys effectively exercise “control of the narrative” in Isabela.
“If you control the narrative, you decide what people focus on, what seems important, and what [should be] ignored,” they explained.
For JM Dela Cruz*, a political science student and an Isabela native, breaking this hold remains a monumental challenge unless an opposing force emerges with equal resources.

“They have built such popularity and reputation in the province. Hindi birong banggain ang ganyang kalaking pamilya. (It’s no joke to take on a family that huge.) It would take someone with the same great influence and machinery to match them in the elections,” Dela Cruz said.
Back in 2004, Padaca commented on the extent of the family’s influence: “Dumating na sa punto sa Isabela, kahit aso ang patakbuhin ng mga Dy ay mananalo kasi ganun sila ka-powerful.”
(It got to the point in Isabela where even if the Dys let a dog run for a government position, it would still win because they’re that powerful.)
Two decades later, that assessment continues to define the political landscape of Isabela. – Rappler.com
*Not their real names

articles.title: No longer taboo, Canada's defence industry steps into Europe's spotlight
articles.summary: At Poland's massive MSPO arms fair, Canada arrives as the 'lead nation' with 230 firms. But shifting decades of reliance on the American market won't be easy.

image.caption: Canada is the 'lead nation' for the 2026 International Defence Industry Exhibition (MSPO) in Kielce, Poland. It's part of Canada's effort to pivot defence sales away from the United States to Europe. (Katie Pedersen/CBC)

blocks.text: The future of warfare is on sale in Poland this week, wrapped in a bright red Canadian maple leaf.

For the first time, Canada is the "lead nation" at a major European defence trade fair, known as MSPO, in Kielce, Poland. It's bringing together more than 230 companies and associations at the exhibition’s Canada Pavillion.
The nation’s oversized presence is framed by red and white banners bearing the Government of Canada logo and punctuated by the occasional sound of military bagpipers for added ambience.
Europe is rearming, mobilizing up to 800 billion euros ($1.3 billion Cdn) for defence over the next three years.

items: Canada was prepared to send ships to Iraq in 2003 if UN approved action, records show
Trump to Canadian plane maker Bombardier: You can't sell in U.S. unless you build in U.S.

blocks.text: One of the pillars of that initiative is known as SAFE, or Security Action for Europe. Canada is the only non-European nation invited to participate, allowing it to bid on European defence contracts as it pledges ongoing support for Ukraine’s defence industrial base.

Charles Barlow, the CEO of Ottawa-based Robotics Centre, says he has been staggered by the change in Canada’s positioning and its sudden eagerness to embrace industries that were shunned only a couple of years ago.
"Defence was a dirty word. [Federal] trade commissioners wouldn’t help," said Barlow during an interview at his booth at the trade fair.
Canada takes the lead at international defence expo
But a trade war with the United States and Canada's push to diversify its key industries away from its largest trading partner has dramatically altered the landscape.
"It's a very big breakthrough as we extend our reach into Europe," said Defence Minister David McGuinty, who was in Kielce on Tuesday to officially kick off the event.

"We are diversifying, we are taking our next steps, we are open to serious negotiation with the United States, but right now this is about our communities, it's about our workers and it's about giving rise to an expanded and greater energy when it comes to our defence sector," he said.
Several Canadian exhibitors told CBC News they would not have been able to make the trip to Poland without financial help provided by the Carney government.
Now that the taboo on financing, marketing and publicly advocating for defence tech has faded away, the industry is trying to quickly pivot to take advantage.
Barlow’s company, which makes small drones and quad copters, has literally taken off in the last year, thanks in part to new deals with European customers.
It's about to move from its current headquarters near Lansdowne Park in Ottawa to a new 32,000-square-foot facility in Kanata.
"A year ago, we were 15 people. Today, we're 56," he said.
One reason for the success of his quadcopters is the innovative use of unconventional materials initially demanded by Canada’s Department of Defence that is now attracting interest elsewhere.
"We've actually manufactured [the drone body] out of plywood. It flies just as well as the carbon-fibre version, which surprised all of us," Barlow said.
Other components — such as a camera, guidance system and the payload — are easily snapped onto the lightweight frame.

Government figures suggest Canada’s defence industry contributes $10 billion to the country’s economy and supports more than 81,000 jobs. The government’s new Defence Industrial Strategy aims to create more than 125,000 new jobs over the next decade.
Red and white banners and maple leaves may help with branding, but cracking the European market is fraught with significant challenges.

"It's a hard market," said Christyn Cianfarani, CEO of the Canadian Defence and Security Industries Association (CADSI). "A lot of the companies in the [Canada] pavilion are small- to medium-sized businesses. It's very hard for a small business to sell directly to a very large government."
Carney touts increasing defence spending as Trump threatens Greenland at NATO summit

She says government help is often essential. For example, if Canada buys something from a European nation and a Canadian company gets involved in the deal, it thereby becomes part of European supply chains.

"Canada recently announced it is going to make a purchase of submarines and the Germans have committed to pulling Canadian firms, Canadian companies, into their supply chains — that's a great way to do it," Cianfarani said.
But Cianfarani says the gravitational pull of the United States — far and away the world’s largest defence spender — remains strong.

"Pivoting from the United States, where it's over 50 per cent of our market share, is not an easy pivot for Canadian business. The U.S. is close, it's in the same time zone and our relationship under NORAD has given us privileges."
David Lord of Zeal Motor, based in Bromont, Que., is among those in Poland trying to navigate that huge leap this week.

His company makes enormous all-terrain vehicles, known as Fat Trucks. With giant buoyant rubber wheels and a flexible chassis, these trucks are highly equipped for Arctic conditions and conducting search and rescue operations in challenging terrain.

Lord says he’s had buyers in Canada, the United States and Great Britain, but the company now has its sights set on Europe, which is proving to be as hard a slog as some of the terrain the Fat Trucks move through.
One of the biggest challenges, he says, is simply showing the vehicle to would-be buyers.
"If you're selling software [to Europe], it's easy. But here, you've got to carry a piece of equipment that's 21,000 pounds across [the ocean]. It is a lot of investment."
"There's nothing like experiencing driving it and conquering terrain, and that's where we're trying to go right now," said Lord.
Beyond the steep shipping costs and logistical hurdles, Canadian companies are landing in a European market that has been fundamentally rewired by the war in Ukraine.
The conflict has shattered decades of peacetime complacency, forcing European militaries to realize that the old, agonizingly slow ways of buying weapons no longer work.
For Canadian firms to succeed here, they have to match a continent moving at lightning speed.
"The procurement system for everybody is changing very quickly, especially for equipment that is rapidly iterating," said Barlow, the Ottawa drone manufacturer.

"It's not like the old days when you could sit down, design a ship, start building it and take it into service eight years after you conceived of it. Now, we have to get it out within eight months. And that speed is actually accelerating."
For companies like Robotics Centre, competing against heavily subsidized European rivals on their own turf is the new, high-stakes normal.
"That's the environment that we're living in right now," Barlow said.

articles.title: Canadian bank CEOs can't stop bragging about AI. Will they kill jobs?
articles.summary: According to a study by Toronto Metropolitan University, 98 per cent of financial sector workers are highly exposed to AI technologies. However, at least one Canadian bank expects its human headcount…

image.caption: TD, BMO, CIBC, RBC, and Scotiabank are the five biggest banks in Canada. (CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

According to a study by Toronto Metropolitan University, 98 per cent of financial sector workers are highly exposed to AI technologies. However, at least one Canadian bank expects its human headcount to rise.
The big banks have more than double the headcount of Canada's auto assembly and parts manufacturing industry

Scotiabank CEO Scott Thomson says artificial intelligence saved his bank roughly 24,000 days' worth of work over about four and a half months. At TD Bank, CEO Raymond Chun recently said AI has reduced the time it takes to pre-process mortgages from about 15 hours to three minutes.

Canada's Big Five banks employ nearly 400,000 full-time-equivalent workers. That's more than double the number of employees in Canada's auto assembly and parts manufacturing industry. TD Bank workers alone outnumber Canada's active military force.

According to a study by Toronto Metropolitan University, 98 per cent of financial sector workers are highly exposed to AI technologies. That's far higher, they say, than the 56 per cent estimated for the Canadian workforce overall.

items: 'Measured confidence': RBC, TD Bank, CIBC share optimistic outlook for Canada's economy

blocks.text: Last month, the Bank of Canada estimated that one‑third of jobs may "undergo substantial changes" because of AI integration, given today's capabilities. The central bank found that banking, insurance and other financial clerks are among the most exposed.

"AI is a big opportunity for us, a transformational opportunity both from an effectiveness, and an efficiency perspective," Thomson said on Wednesday at the annual Scotiabank Financials Summit in Toronto.
His enthusiasm is shared by his C-suite peers.

"There isn't a part of our business that's not being impacted by AI," RBC CEO Dave McKay told an audience at an industry conference hosted by his bank earlier this year. At an event in June, he spoke about using AI every morning to generate custom reports based on RBC's internal data.

Last month, BMO CEO Darryl White said predictive AI modelling in his bank's insurance business can make underwriting decisions in as little as 10 seconds. The industry standard is at least 28 days, he noted.

Stock market analyst John Aiken covers the banking industry for New York-based Jefferies Financial Group. He sees top executives at Canada's Big Five — Royal Bank, TD Bank, Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank, and National Bank — brimming with excitement over the billions of dollars they've invested in AI in recent years.
What's unclear, he said, is how rank-and-file bank employees will feel the impact.
"This isn't a little pet project," Aiken told CBC News. "The funny thing is, it's the CEOs themselves that are bringing it up unprompted."
"Strangely enough, we're not seeing headcount reductions from the banks," he said. "You're presumably going to see lesser demand for lower skilled workers ... the front-line staff at the branches."
Questions about how AI will affect some of Canada's largest private employers come amid a much broader debate over how the technology could shape humanity as a whole.

Earlier this week, an artificial intelligence researcher quit his job at Anthropic, accusing the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, of irresponsibly "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence." On Tuesday, another Anthropic employee wrote on the social media platform X that, "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade."
On Wednesday, federal AI Minister Evan Solomon said "there are real concerns" at the frontier of AI development
Existential warnings about AI 'are not new,' minister says

Jon Pinkus, a partner at Samfiru Tamakin LLP who specializes in employment law, sees jobs at risk throughout the white-collar world because of AI. However, he said he has yet to see a clear-cut instance of humans being replaced.
"I have real generational anxieties for the incoming workforce. Not just this generation, but for generations to come," he said.
"I think there are going to be certain positions that just don't exist, particularly more junior positions, entry-level positions," Pinkus said.
"A lot of those entry level tasks are the ones now being done by AI ... [it does] them well enough for many organizations to say, 'Why are we going to pay this person $80,000 per year?'"

Jeff Lanthier, director of media relations at RBC, told CBC News in response to questions about AI's impact on the bank's headcount that people and relationships will always be at the core of the bank's strategy.
"We see AI as an enhancement, not a replacement," Lanthier said.
The other Big Five banks did not respond to requests for comment in time for publication.

At its investor day last year, RBC announced plans to generate $700 million to $1 billion in enterprise value through AI-driven benefits by 2027. TD Bank is similarly targeting $1 billion in annual value from its artificial intelligence initiatives. Both banks have in-house AI research labs, called RBC Borealis and Layer 6, respectively.
CIBC CEO sees human headcount rising
CIBC CEO Harry Culham said his bank's new AI workspace is more like a "co-worker" than a chatbot. Even so, he predicts the bank will add employees overall.

"We actually see headcount growth over the next five years," CIBC CEO Harry Culham said on his bank's Aug. 27 earnings call with stock market analysts. "We're using it all over the entire organization, and we've got thousands and thousands of people being educated."
Kiridaran Kanagaretnam, an associate dean at York University's Schulich School of Business, sees the Canadian banking industry's overall headcount drifting higher, absent a major financial crisis.
He recommends students pursue professional designations in accounting and finance to boost their value to employers.
"Everything is changing at a rapid rate," he said. "But that doesn't mean things are bleak."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. He was also a Columbia University energy journalism fellow for 2025.

articles.title: ‘Why did you go to school that day?’: Mother of Dawson shooting victim reflects 20 years later
articles.summary: Louise De Sousa lost her daughter Anastasia in the Dawson College shooting in Montreal nearly 20 years ago. She reflects on the anniversary of her death, memories she has of her daughter and working…

image.caption: Louise De Sousa lost her daughter Anastasia in the Dawson College shooting nearly 20 years ago. She stands next to photographs of her late child and her other children. (Josianne Létourneau/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal

Louise De Sousa lost her daughter Anastasia in the Dawson College shooting in Montreal nearly 20 years ago. She reflects on the anniversary of her death, memories she has of her daughter and working through grief.
Louise De Sousa still lives with the what-ifs 2 decades after daughter's death
The grief of losing her daughter in a mass shooting at Montreal's Dawson College has weighed heavily on Louise De Sousa for nearly two decades.
As the 20th anniversary of the shooting approaches, De Sousa still finds herself wondering about the life her daughter Anastasia might have lived.
The what-ifs surface on ordinary days, but especially during family milestones, including births and weddings.
“You always think back on that day and the what-ifs. Where would she have been in her life career-wise, married, children?” De Sousa wonders.
If she could speak to her daughter again, there are many things De Sousa says she would tell her. But she would ask one question:
"Why did you go to school that day, why didn't you skip?"
Sept. 13: The last day
In her living room, surrounded by photographs of her loved ones, including some of Anastasia, De Sousa recalls the last morning she saw her daughter alive.
On Sept. 13, 2006, she went into her 18-year-old’s bubblegum-pink bedroom and asked if she wanted a ride to school, but Anastasia didn’t need one.
Later that day, a man would enter the school and open fire, killing Anastasia and injuring 19 people.
De Sousa first learned about the shooting from coworkers while she was having lunch in her workplace cafeteria.
She and other family members tried calling Anastasia, but there was no answer.

items: What's changed, and what hasn't since the Dawson shooting
'Sadness, homage and hope' one year after Dawson shooting

blocks.text: De Sousa went to the hospital after learning that injured people had been taken there. Hours passed and it was at 9 p.m. that she received confirmation that Anastasia had died.
“That night when we came home, I remember we were all crying. You could hear everybody crying in their bed and I'm waiting for the door to open to say: “Mom, I'm here,” De Sousa said.
Living with grief
The days that followed her death were “a daze.” But thankfully, De Sousa had her family.
For her, moving through grief has meant going to therapy with her husband and supporting one another in the family.
Every year, De Sousa and her immediate family gather at the cemetery with Hayder Kadhim — a survivor of the Dawson shooting who was shot in the head — and his family.
For De Sousa, being surrounded by people who knew her daughter — and her granddaughters who never got to meet "Auntie Anastasia" — brings comfort.
They take a moment to stand together and talk to her; a ritual De Sousa carries into her home, too.
De Sousa says she talks to Anastasia every night.
“There's not a day that goes by without her, without thinking of her or talking to her,” she said.
“I can't fall asleep at night if I don't speak to her.”
And what she misses most is her daughter’s laugh.
“She had this laughter that was so contagious. She would start laughing and, to tell a story, sometimes she never got through her story. But you were laughing now.”
Keeping Anastasia’s spirit alive
Although Anastasia has been gone for nearly two decades, De Sousa says she still feels her presence around the house.
In the smell of her perfume – even when no one has sprayed it. In the bubblegum-pink strip of paint the family left in Anastasia’s room after repainting it. In the songs she used to listen to.
“I hear songs from Sean Paul and all these old songs that she used to love back in the early 2000s and I see her singing it with her sister and her brother,” De Sousa said.
Sometimes, she says, she sees shadows or hears someone call out “Mom” when she is alone in the house.
“I always tell myself: 'Oh OK, she's in here. She came.'”
At times, De Sousa even places an extra plate on the table, absentmindedly, and leaves it there when she realizes what she’s done.
Channeling grief into advocacy
After her daughter’s death, De Sousa became an advocate with PolySeSouvient — a prominent Canadian gun-control advocacy group founded in 1989 following the École Polytechnique massacre in Montreal.
She believes the government should do more regarding gun control.
“Depending on the government we have, we do two steps back, one step forward, then you know, they stop. I find it should be a lot more severe,” she said.

items: 10 years after Dawson shooting, killer's weapon is more accessible than in 2006

blocks.text: De Sousa also remains in contact with survivors of the shooting, some of whom she’s close to.
“She passed away. But there's also 19 other victims that their lives, I'm sure, have been adjusted and not easy," she said.
And De Sousa remains determined to ensure that the shooting — and Anastasia — are never forgotten.
“I want people to remember what happened. And I want those students to know what happened in their school. It's part of history,” she said.
“We’ve got to remember what happened. We’ve got to try and do better.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Hénia Ould-Hammou is a Montreal journalist with CBC News. She previously completed an internship with La Presse after graduating from McGill University with a double major in political science and psychology. Hénia is interested in international and societal issues, community stories, soccer, politics and rap. You can send her an email at henia.ould-hammou@cbc.ca
With files from CBC's Sean Henry

articles.title: TIFF's at a turning point — but how will the film festival's new focus on dealmaking affect fans?
articles.summary: As the 51st edition of the Toronto International Film Festival rolls out the red carpet, the country's largest film festival is changing. With other festivals snagging buzzy world premieres, TIFF is…

image.caption: The Toronto International Film Festival is an annual draw for film fans who pack theatres and crowd red carpets to get a glimpse of glitzy celebs, but TIFF has been reinventing itself as a place where movie deals are made. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·Analysis

As the 51st edition of the Toronto International Film Festival rolls out the red carpet, the country's largest film festival is changing. With other festivals snagging buzzy world premieres, TIFF is reinventing itself as a place for making movie deals. But will this transformation combined with higher ticket prices hurt TIFF's tastemaker reputation?
Why this transformation, combined with higher ticket prices, could change TIFF's tastemaker reputation
For years, the Toronto International Festival has prided itself as a tastemaker. Toronto was the place movie stars flocked to for the unofficial start of their Oscar campaigns.
But as major films and A-list stars increasingly look to other festivals as launchpads, TIFF is reinventing itself with a new focus on the business of buying and packaging movies.

In a tumultuous time for the industry, this transformation could help keep TIFF in the conversation, but as ticket prices rise, what does it all mean for the heart of this festival: the filmgoing public?
Here's a look at TIFF's very own movie makeover moment — plus a few choice films you may want to catch yourself.
Shifting the spotlight to dealmaking

Continuing a post-pandemic trend, many of the season's buzziest titles, including Primetime starring Robert Pattinson and You Can See Everything from Canada's own Nathan Fielder, chose Venice or Telluride over TIFF for their world premieres.

So, like the nerdy girl in a rom-com who takes off her glasses, TIFF is trying to transform itself, pivoting to embrace the dealmaking and caffeine-fuelled strategy sessions that populate many major festivals.
Launching with a $23 million boost from Ottawa, TIFF: The Market features 70 sessions and events exploring film, television and interactive content.

A sci-fi film with Russell Crowe and Priyanka Chopra, a rom-com featuring Colin Firth and Halle Berry and a new instalment of the Air Bud franchise are just a few of the projects being shopped around town.
But just like the cutthroat competition for red carpet premieres, TIFF will be facing competition from other industry players.
First, there's the Cannes marketplace, the biggest and best known showcase that sets the tempo for the year.

Case in point, it was on La Croisette, the famous boulevard at the centre of Cannes, where the buzz began for Jordan Firstman's Club Kid, resulting in a frenzied bidding war. That film's Canadian premiere takes place at TIFF Sunday.
The Trump factor
While TIFF is trying to position itself as a fall alternative to spring's Cannes, it's also competing with the American Film Market (AFM), which takes place in November in Los Angeles.
While AFM generally caters to more mainstream films, TIFF, which has always touted international cinema, will be highlighting emerging markets in Africa and Asia as part of The Market programming.

And as U.S. President Donald Trump talks up new national incentives to reshore American film production, international buyers wary of engaging with Hollywood or even looking to avoid hassles at the border, may see TIFF as an attractive alternative.
Tickets and tastemakers

As TIFF's star wattage continues to diminish and the festival evolves to become more business-facing, questions remain about what that means for the heart of the TIFF experience: the film fans. The ones who camp out in long lines, wait for hours to watch stars walk red carpets and scream like pirates at midnight screenings.
Every year TIFF rightly boasts about its track record of predicting best picture winners, touting the People's Choice Award as a barometer of Oscar worthiness.
But as ticket prices climb higher (regular screenings now begin at $30 and up), fewer members of the public who make the festival one big, beautiful focus group end up populating those screenings.

Speaking to the Toronto Star recently, TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey acknowledged that glitzy premieres with stars and filmmakers in attendance command higher ticket prices, but he also argued that they still cost less than a ticket to pro sports games in the city.
At a time when Canadians want to support the home team, that means some film fans could find themselves priced out of a seat.
Must-see movies
While the number of A-listers coming to TIFF may be shrinking, there's still a number of the upcoming fall season's most buzzworthy films making the rounds in Toronto.
Ink finds Trainspotting director Danny Boyle returning to Britain to explore the rise of The Sun tabloid newspaper, with rumoured James Bond contender Jack O'Connell as a rapacious editor in chief.

Then there's The Debut, a love letter to community theatre written and directed by actor Jesse Eisenberg. In 2025 Eisenberg's A Real Pain helped Kieran Culkin bring home Oscar gold. Already, some are seeing a golden hue in Julianne Moore's performance as a harried housewife who abandons herself in a role.
Primetime programming

Increasingly, TIFF has embraced both the small and big screen in its programming and this year a number of TV series are showcased in the Primetime program. That includes Apple TV's Slow Horses, which is bringing its sixth season premiere to Toronto with star Gary Oldman, who will also be interviewed on stage.

With shooting already underway for the second season of Heated Rivalry, another hot title is the upcoming Crave series Yaga, starring Hudson Williams as an heir to a powerful fishery and The Matrix's Carrie-Anne Moss as a university professor. Riffing on the fearsome fairy tale character Baba Yaga, the show promises a steamy mix of mischief and malevolence.
Oh Canada

It's worth remembering that, before the trade war escalated, the Canadian film industry was riding high, based on the success of films like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, Mile End Kicks, undertone and more.

To capitalize on the moment, there's a broad swath of Canadian titles at TIFF this year. Can't get enough of Jay Baruchel and love Canadian hosers who perform incredible feats? From FUBAR director Michael Dowse comes The Stunt Driver, which explores the true story of Canadian stuntman Ken Carter.

Music fans can check out Neil Peart: No One's Disciple, a 106 minute documentary exploring the life of the late Rush drummer with the help of Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer Chad Smith and Stewart Copeland of The Police.

If you'd like a less conventional film, Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney promises an unhinged look at the former prime minister. Director Matthew Rankin, who also helmed Universal Language, has conjured what TIFF describes as a "retro-pop fever dream," which will be premiering in the always raucous Midnight Madness category.
Not content to let Heated Rivalry steal all the hockey shenanigans, Smudge the Blades is a scrappy sports story about an Indigenous hockey team based in Northern Alberta.
Triple threat Cree director/writer/star Cody Lightning plays the team's beleaguered coach alongside an all-star team of Indigenous talent including Jana Schmieding and Paulina Alexis.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Eli Glasner is the senior entertainment reporter and screentime columnist for CBC News. Covering culture has taken him from the northern tip of Moosonee Ontario to the Oscars and beyond. You can reach him at eli.glasner@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Hospitality industry fears jobs at risk from plan to give mayors powers to impose ‘tourist tax’
articles.summary:
The sector is concerned by reports that there won’t be a cap on the levy that can be imposed by mayors

Good morning. Last year Andy Burnham, who was then mayor of Greater Manchester, and his…

blocks.text: The sector is concerned by reports that there won’t be a cap on the levy that can be imposed by mayors
LIVE Updated 1m ago
Andy Burnham in row with hospitality sector

Good morning. Last year Andy Burnham, who was then mayor of Greater Manchester, and his close friend and ally Steve Rotheram, mayor of the Liverpool city region, were urging the government to allow mayors in England to bring in what they called a visitor levy.
Burnham and Rotheram were pushing at an open door. In May this year Keir Starmer included plans for an overnight visitor levy bill in the king’s speech.
Scotland and Wales already have their own versions of this.
Now Burnham’s government is about to announce further details of the plan. The Daily Telegraph has the story.

blocks.caption: Telegraph splash Photograph: Daily Telegraph

blocks.text: In May the government was not specific about whether or not there would be a cap on how high the levy could go. In their Telegraph story, Szu Ping Chan, Harry Brennan and Eir Nolsøe say the plans being announced by the government will be more extensive than the hospitality industry expected. They report:

double quotation markOfficials stunned the hospitality industry late on Wednesday by announcing that English mayors and other local leaders will be able to impose an uncapped “overnight visitor levy” on anyone staying in hotels, holiday lets and bed and breakfasts. Bosses said they had been led to believe that the levy would be capped, as is the case in Wales. However, England will now follow the Scottish model, where there is technically no upper limit on what can be charged.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, told the paper: “An unlimited tourist tax would be hugely limiting for the chances of the young people who might otherwise be employed in tourism and hospitality.”
This morning Allen Simpson, chief executive of UK Hospitality, the trade body for the sector, claimed that this proposal would cost thousands of jobs. He told the Today programme:

double quotation markWhat we’re talking about here is an open-ended power for mayors to set tourism taxes at any level they want. Remember, if you go to Paris, if you go to Rome, if you go to Berlin, you’re paying a small tourism tax, but it’s capped. This one isn’t. And VAT is only 10%. So even before England introduces this new tax, the tax on a holiday in the UK is already more expensive than our peers.
When it was put to him that mayors would not have to introduce this tax, Simpson accepted that. But he went on:

double quotation markWe know that local government is struggling for funds. It was hit very hard by austerity. And if you only devolve one tax-raising power, of course local mayors are going to pull that lever till it snaps. If it’s a 5% tax, which is entirely possible, that’s what it is in Edinburgh – but that’s lower than it is in, say, Aberdeen – the economic analysis is that it’s 33,000 jobs which will go.

Simpson said UK Hospitality was able to come up with a specific figure because the sector could measure quite precisely what impact price has on demand. He also claimed taxes on the hospitality sector were already very high.
Simpson went on:

double quotation markFor anyone who takes a holiday in the UK, it’s going to be an average of about £100, £120, on the cost of a family holiday, which is more than double the benefit from the energy VAT cut that we saw earlier in the year. So it is not going to be painless.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: NHS England publishes its monthly hospital performance figures.
9.30am: The actor Michael Sheen gives evidence to the Commons Welsh affairs committee about contaminated land, a topic he investigated for a highly-praised documentary.

Morning: Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, chairs a meeting with regional mayors from No 10 North to discuss plans for a tourism tax. Later Lucy Powell, the education secretary, hosts a summit there on making England a “technical education superpower”.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 11.30am: Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, is due to make a statement to MPs about Ukraine and the threat from Russia.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

In a statement, impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol said that as of 2 p.m., the participation of the following legal luminaries to physically appear before the court on September 16 to present their expert opinions has been “successfully secured:”
Retired Supreme Court Chief (SC) Justice Artemio Panganiban Retired SC Chief Justice Reynato Puno Retired SC Associate Justice Adolf Azcuna

items: 12m agoMorning opening: Russian attacks continue as Zelenskyy continues diplomacy tour

blocks.text: Morning opening: Russian attacks continue as Zelenskyy continues diplomacy tour

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
At least nine people died in overnight Russian strikes on Ukraine, targeting warehouses and ports across the country.
Five people were reported dead and 24 injured in the Sumy region, with four killed and 19 injured in a separate attack on Ukraine’s Black Sea port of Mykolaiv.
The latest wave of attacks come as president Volodymyr Zelenskyy continues his international diplomacy tour with talks on air defence and winter preparations in Canada.

blocks.caption: President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, arrive in Calgary, Canada. Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: In a statement this morning, he highlighted Ukraine’s ability to conduct retaliatory strikes against Russia, as he said:

“Over the past 24 hours, our warriors struck eight Russian infrastructure facilities supporting the war. An oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region and a seaport in Dagestan were hit. Sites in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan, and Bryansk regions were also struck. Russia continues its daily terror against Ukraine. And every day, it receives a just response. I thank every warrior and everyone who enables our long-range capabilities and precision.”

Late last night, Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Støre said that Zelenskyy’s plane was almost hit by a drone when leaving Moldova for Oslo earlier this week. “That is just the reality he lives in,” he told broadcaster NRK.
The alleged incident happened during a previously reported drone incursion into Moldova and Romania on Tuesday night (Europe Live, Tuesday). The Ukrainian side did not comment on what happened.

Separately, Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte is meeting with Germany’s foreign minister Johann Wadephul this morning, with the pair set to discuss Ukraine and Germany’s own experience with Russia in recent weeks after an attempted drone attack in Leipzig.
I will bring you the key lines from their talks, and other news across Europe.
It’s Thursday, 10 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Germany 'rebuilding pillars' of national security
articles.summary: Germany's interior minister has defended plans to give security agencies greater investigative powers to counter hybrid threats. Meanwhile, German inflation rose as the ECB reconsiders interest…

image.caption: A search was launched for more explosive drones after one was found at Leipzig/Halle AirportImage: Sebastian Willnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 10, 2026
Dobrindt warns of growing threats to German security

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has defended plans to give security authorities greater investigative powers, accusing critics of putting people's safety at risk amid what he described as a heightened threat to Germany.
Speaking during a parliamentary debate on his ministry's 2027 budget, Dobrindt, of the conservative Christian Social Union, said the proposed powers were necessary to "protect our freedom."
"The threat level is high and is coming from different places," Dobrindt said.

He pointed to an explosives-laden drone discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport as evidence of the security challenges facing Germany, adding that Russia was clearly behind the incident and that it was "not an isolated event."

Dobrindt has pushed for stronger measures against drones and hybrid threats. He said under his leadership, the federal and state governments have established a new joint drone defense center, while a Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats (GAZ Hybrid) opened in June.
"We are rebuilding the pillars of security architecture," Dobrindt said on Thursday.
The Interior Ministry's budget is set to increase by more than €950 million ($1.1 billion) to €16.7 billion ($19.5 billion).
The Federal Criminal Police Office and Federal Police are among the agencies set to receive additional personnel.
Germany's Federal Office for Information Security, which is responsible for cybersecurity, is also due to receive more funding.

Sonja Eichwede, deputy parliamentary leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party, highlighted additional spending planned for the Federal Agency for Technical Relief, saying it was important for civil protection and disaster response.

articles.title: Trafficked into fraud: An African crisis in Cambodia
articles.summary: Southeast Asia has long emerged as a major hub of highly organized online fraud operations, targeting people all around the world. According to the United Nations, these operations generate tens of…

blocks.text: Southeast Asia has long emerged as a major hub of highly organized online fraud operations, targeting people all around the world.

According to the United Nations, these operations generate tens of billions of dollars annually, having long surpassed the illegal drug trade as the most profitable activity for criminal networks, as reported by the United States Institute of Peace.

However, those who fall prey to scams and other fraudulent activities aren’t the only victims of these criminal rings; alone in Southeast Asia, the scam industry is powered by at least 300,000 trafficked workers from 66 countries. They are routinely subjected to torture, sexual abuse and forced labor, according to a recent UN Human Rights report.

African nationals now form the largest group of those trafficked to and stranded in countries like Myanmar and Cambodia, without any viable pathway to go back home, says the NGO Freedom Collaborative.
In Cambodia, one of the main obstacles to helping stranded Africans return home is that many countries on the continent, such as Uganda, Liberia, Ghana and Nigeria, lack consular representation.
But there are other reasons.
“Some countries have zero interest,” says Montse Ferrer, co-regional director of Amnesty International, who also blames the home countries for their inaction.
“They’re not even picking up the phone, let alone providing the paperwork or the money for them to go back.”
Cambodia’s reluctant crackdown on scam operators

Ferrer believes that the Cambodian government also has an interest in keeping scam trafficking victims in the country. This is because many of the victims now have overstay fines for their visas against their names in Cambodia, reaching thousands of dollars in many instances.
“They don’t allow NGOs to provide the support these people need, and instead they have resorted to arresting and threatening them,” Ferrer told DW.

Following great pressure from the international community — including threats of financial sanctions by the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the European Union — Cambodia did eventually agree to launch a crackdown on the scamming industry earlier this year.
According to the Cambodian Ministry of Information, the initiative resulted in many arrests and triggered a mass exodus of dubious operatives from scamming industry.

But the crackdown also created a secondary crisis: Thousands of trafficked foreign workers remain stranded in the country without documentation nor legal status; now, they also lack shelter and money in many instances, NGOs say.
Many who have sought help in Cambodia have reportedly been placed in immigration detention, while others have to sleep rough and beg for food.
Instead of being given protection, trafficking victims often face stigmatization and abuse on the street of the capital Phnom Penh and elsewhere.
Lured to Cambodia under false pretenses
Emmanuel David is one of those stuck in Cambodia. The 28-year-old Liberian national arrived there in 2025 after a treacherous irregular journey originating in Vietnam.
“My friend told me there was work in Cambodia, but he did not explain that it was scamming work,” David explained.
The scamming company had offered him a lucrative deal of making around $800 (€700) per month, which is more than double the average wage for qualified individuals in Liberia.
The reality hit quite differently: Once there, David was forced to work 14 hours a day to deceive women on various dating apps to part with their money.
But David was initially unable — and later unwilling — to meet the set target quota of scams per day.
In response, the criminal group he worked for started billing him for food and accommodation through his wages and later even confiscated his belongings, including his passport.
David says he also faced substantial physical violence, including beatings, for four months.
Eventually, he left “with no documents and no money,” and is now hoping to find a way back to Liberia.
His story is far from unique.
‘Hundreds’ of Africans trafficked to criminal compounds
Another survivor, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, also recounted how he was “beaten and [subjected to] electric shocks.”
The abuse resulted in him having to be hospitalized for three weeks, and he is now unable to pay his medical bills.
Pia Oberoi, chief of the Right to Development Section at UN Human Rights, told DW that “despite the promise of a good salary, most come out in debt.”

She also confirmed that a growing number of trafficking victims in Southeast Asia come from African countries, “because there is clearly a recruitment industry that’s built around Africa, targeting African nationals.”
Other victims have corroborated this development, describing hundreds of Africans packed into heavily fortified compounds.
“Once you’re inside there’s no way out,” an informant, who also chose to remain anonymous, told DW.
He said the compounds have their own laws, and that sexual abuse and psychological violence are an integral part of how they operate.
The police, he says, just turn a blind eye.
No government assistance from any direction
Amnesty International speaks of an unfolding humanitarian crisis, warning that escapees are widely being treated as criminals rather than as trafficking victims, a sentiment the UN shares.
“They shouldn’t be punished for crimes they were forced to commit,” the UN’s Oberoi highlights.
Several of the victims contacted by DW meanwhile said their governments were notably “slow” to help with their repatriation.
DW also attempted to contact several African foreign ministries for comment but has yet to receive a response.

A statement issued by the Cambodian government meanwhile said that more than 700 compounds run chiefly by Chinese nationals had been raided, with 58,266 foreign nationals deported and nearly 30,000 suspects arrested over the past year.
However, the Cambodian government did not reply to DW’s direct request for further information.

The UN’s International Organization for Migration (IOM) explained it’s trying its utmost to help the trafficking victims; but in the face of severe budgetary constraints, it can only provide “limited, prioritized support.”
Fear, guilt and stigma
Humanitarian groups also warn of a high risk of victims being re-trafficked. This is a danger even for those who have somehow managed to return to their countries of origin.
In some instances, those who come back home are stigmatized as a failure — “a situation that is really unbearable,” says Ferrer.
Emmanuel David is a prime example: He feels obliged to to apologize to his family for not returning a success.
When asked about his little daughter, he simply says “Daddy can’t go home without money.” /dl

articles.title: Putin rejects mobilization rumors, many Russians unconvinced
articles.summary: Twice within the first week of September, Russian President Vladimir Putin publicly dismissed rumors of a looming mobilization campaign in the country. On September 1, Putin called the rumors…

blocks.text: Twice within the first week of September, Russian President Vladimir Putin publicly dismissed rumors of a looming mobilization campaign in the country. On September 1, Putin called the rumors “complete nonsense” and described them as an “information attack” against Russia.
Two days later, on September 3, at the Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Putin said that “there is no scenario today that would require mobilization.”
Summons are cause for unease among Russian DW users

DW’s Russian service asked readers in Russia, on condition of anonymity, whether they see signs of an impending mobilization. The most common response from DW readers concerned receiving summonses from military enlistments offices.
“My nephew received a summons for data verification,” wrote a reader from the industrial city of Naberezhnye Chelny.
“I received a summons ordering me to appear for data verification. I’m self-employed. What should I do?” wrote a user named Maxim.
“One of my friends, a school teacher, received a summons through the government services portal [Gosuslugi] on July 9 to update his records,” said another reader, Sergei.

People fear that they may be called up for military service or lose the ability to leave the country freely. As a result, some of those who have received draft notices are seeking to travel abroad as quickly as possible, while restrictions on leaving the country have not yet taken effect.
“One acquaintance of mine left Russia two months ago after receiving a summons for data verification from the military enlistment office,” one reader wrote.
Emigration as ‘a fantasy’
Not everyone, however, sees emigration as a realistic option in the event of mobilization.
“As for leaving, that’s a fantasy. Where would you go, and more importantly, with what money?” one DW reader wrote.

In June, reports emerged from Russia’s Penza region that men were forcibly taken to military enlistment offices and pressured into signing military contracts. According to local reports, the practice became widespread enough that residents organized protests in support of relatives and neighbors. Journalists reporting on the issue say such raids are continuing.

“People are being detained, particularly near the entrances to their apartment buildings,” Lena Lemyasova, a journalist with news outlet Important Stories [Vazhnye Istorii], told DW. “Often men who have been drinking. Unknown individuals approach them, or vehicles pull up — often cars provided by local authorities. The men are simply seized and taken away, then their families and neighbors hear nothing more. Later, information sometimes emerges that they were transported to military units. They are often held there before being sent to the front.”
Important Stories specializes in investigative journalism. Its publisher, Roman Anin, spent ten years as investigations editor at well-known independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta.
What do Russian lawyers say about the summonses?

Does receiving a military summons mean a person will be sent to war? According to lawyer Artem Klyga, a summons issued “for data verification” does not in itself mean that someone will be drafted, mobilized or deployed. Data verification notices are one of several legally established reasons for calling someone to a military enlistment office.

“These summonses only show that military enlistment offices have significantly improved their military registration procedures. If mobilization begins, such records would help authorities quickly summon the people they need,” Klyga explained to DW.

Russians have also increasingly reported receiving mobilization orders issued in advance. In peacetime, such orders do not oblige individuals to take any action. However, if mobilization is declared, recipients are required to report to their designated military enlistment office.

“They were issued before the war and during the war [against Ukraine] as well. But what changed in the first half of 2026 is that, judging by all indications, they began to be distributed in the hundreds of thousands,” Russian lawyer Timofei Vaskin told DW. “We do not know the exact figures because the information is classified. But judging from social media reports and the number of inquiries we and our colleagues received, the increase was dramatic, by dozens of times.”
At the same time, the 2022 decree on partial mobilization in Russia has never been formally revoked and technically remains in force.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has repeatedly described reports of a new mobilization wave as “fake stories.” Yet critics note that Peskov also denied reports of a possible mobilization beginning in May 2022.
Just eight days before the announcement of partial mobilization, he said: “At the moment, this is not being discussed.”
Growing demand for mobilization specialists

As of August 8, DW found several vacancies on the Russian job platform HeadHunter seeking specialists in “mobilization preparedness.” 40 such vacancies are available in Moscow and the surrounding region and 13 in St Petersburg.

For example, some companies are looking for specialists responsible for ensuring that the organization has a mobilization plan in place and knows how it would operate if the state were to place the economy on a wartime footing. Their duties also include preparing the company for emergencies and civil defense measures, as well as helping to transition the organization to a special operating regime in the event of wartime conditions.
The positions were advertised by both private companies and state institutions.
Summonses, military training exercises, the expansion of military registration systems and active recruitment efforts help explain why official denials have failed to put the rumors to rest.
Preparing for ‘any decision Putin might make’

“The way to look at this is that bureaucrats have been tasked with preparing the system for any decision Putin might make. And if that decision is mobilization, they are expected to be ready,” Artem Klyga said.

Several cases involving anomalous flood control projects that are being handled by the Sandiganbayan may be completed within the year, Sandiganbayan Presiding Judge Geraldine Econg said Thursday.
During the Judiciary’s budget hearing, Econg said that the first batch of flood control cases filed by the Office of the Ombudsman in November 2025 are already at the defense stage.
“That means that in less than a year, we are already in the defense side. So that’s pretty fast po,” Econg said.
“If we follow the Speedy Trial Act that was enacted by the Supreme Court, we will see the conviction within the year. Or acquittal within the year,” she later added.
She said the Sandiganbayan is currently handling 26 cases tied to the flood control anomalies involving a number of senators and congressmen.
For his part, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian pushed for more funds to be allocated to the Judiciary, noting a P551 million decrease in the Sandiganbayan's funding.
He described the smaller funding as “counterintuitive.”

“Because the focus now actually is on the Sandiganbayan. In fact, we should support the Sandiganbayan more rather than reduce its budget. Because they need to capacitate themselves, make themselves more efficient, get more manpower to support the voluminous cases that are being filed in the Sandigan,” he said.

“So I don’t subscribe to the recommendation by the DBM to reduce it by P551 million. Hindi tama ‘yung oras at hindi tama ‘yung timing na gagawin natin ‘yan. Kita naman natin sa news ang daming cases na fina-file (The time and timing for doing that aren't right. We can see from the news that so many cases are being filed) ,” he added.
The Judiciary is requesting an augmentation of P5.344 billion from its original budget proposal of P86.271 billion.
Meanwhile, Senator Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan asked the Judiciary to submit a document identifying its priorities.
