articles.title: JP Morgan boss Jamie Dimon meets UK PM and chancellor to warn against bank tax hike
articles.summary:
Wall Street billionaire tells Andy Burnham and John Healey ahead of October budget that hike could put investment at risk, it is understood

Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of the largest US…

blocks.text: Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of the largest US bank, JP Morgan, is understood to have warned Andy Burnham and the UK chancellor, John Healey, against raising taxes on banks in his inaugural budget in October.
The Wall Street billionaire met the prime minister and the new chancellor on Wednesday and cautioned them that higher taxes could put investment and employment in the UK at risk, it is understood.
The meeting came amid speculation that Healey is considering a windfall tax on banks and oil companies in his budget on 28 October.
Dimon has a long track record of lobbying against Britain’s additional bank taxes, which were imposed after the government bailed out big UK lenders in the 2008 financial crisis.
Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, as well as a separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets.

The JP Morgan chief executive has previously warned that raising these taxes further could have “adverse consequences”. In August, he told Healey in a telephone conversation that higher levies could hit jobs, citing a fall in finance roles in New York that he blamed on the city’s tax regime.

Dimon was among a group of bank bosses who successfully lobbied against higher taxes before Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves’s budget last year – with Dimon hosting Varun Chandra, who remains in his post as the prime minister’s business envoy, at a birthday celebration for King Charles at the bank’s Manhattan headquarters.
Days afterwards, Dimon announced plans to build a 3m sq ft tower in London’s Canary Wharf district, although he added that a “continuing positive business environment in the UK” was required.

However, in May this year, he said he could scrap plans for the £3bn tower – which is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters and house more than half its 23,000-strong UK workforce – if Keir Starmer were replaced by a new Labour prime minister who was hostile to banks.
after newsletter promotion

Andy Burnham has not made any specific comments about a bank tax so far. However, he has faced calls to introduce higher levies from the TUC and the campaign group Positive Money, which argue a tax increase could help cover rising household bills as part of his drive to tackle the cost of living.
The UK’s four biggest lenders: HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds Banking Group, have generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years, largely off the back of rising interest rates.
UK banks together paid an estimated £43.3bn in tax for the financial year that ended in March 2025, according to a report commissioned by the industry body UK Finance.

articles.title: Primark to offer home delivery as it prepares to split from owner ABF
articles.summary:
Clothing chain says trading in Europe ‘challenging’ but customers are responding well to its price-cutting campaign

Primark will offer home delivery in Britain for the first time, as the…

blocks.text: Primark will offer home delivery in Britain for the first time, as the fast-fashion retailer prepares to spin off from its owner Associated British Foods (ABF).

The clothing chain, which already offers a click and collect service in the UK, has long avoided home delivery, arguing that its low prices made it too difficult to absorb the cost of packing and shipping orders.
However, the company disclosed on Thursday that it had acquired an automated fulfilment facility in Sheffield and would offer home delivery “in the future”.

“Primark’s digital maturity, including the success of click and collect, and online market developments, mean there is now the opportunity for profitable growth through the home delivery channel,” it said in a statement.

The news comes as Primark prepares to split from its parent company ABF, the owner of Twinings tea and Kingsmill bread. The demerger, which is likely to complete in December 2027, is expected to create two new FTSE 100 companies, with analysts predicting that Primark could be valued at as much as £9bn, and the food business £4bn.

The company told investors in an update on Thursday morning that it expected Primark’s sales to drop 3% ⁠in its quarter ended on 12 September, with ​the UK and ​Ireland up 0.4% ​but continental Europe down 4.3%.

George Weston, the chief executive of ABF, said Primark’s trading in Europe “remained challenging”, but the initial customer reaction to its “iconic value” campaign – in which it cut prices across hundreds of autumn and winter products – had been encouraging.
Weston, a member of the billionaire family that controls ABF and who is the long-term chief executive of the group, is to lead the food business after the demerger.
Eoin Tonge, an experienced former ABF, Marks & Spencer and Greencore finance director, will remain as chief executive of Primark.

The fashion chain, which was founded by Arthur Ryan under its Irish brand name, Penneys, in Dublin in 1969, opened its first shop in Britain in 1974, in Derby. It employs more than 80,000 people around the world.

articles.title: Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes
articles.summary: Iranian authorities have launched a clampdown on cafes in the capital, Tehran, in recent months, suspecting them of fostering anti-government sentiment and facilitating protests. According to the…

blocks.text: Iranian authorities have launched a clampdown on cafes in the capital, Tehran, in recent months, suspecting them of fostering anti-government sentiment and facilitating protests.
According to the human rights organization HRANA, at least seven cafes and restaurants were shut down on July 19 alone for allegedly failing to comply with mandatory hijab rules.

Previously, some media outlets, including Javan, a newspaper affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have described cafes as “gathering places for protesters” who, in their view, pose a threat to “national security.”
Most recently, the “Vanak Park” cafes in Tehran were sealed, resulting in at least 200 people losing their jobs.
Crackdown on cafes
Authorities believe cafes, because of their widespread presence and popularity, could play a role in organizing mass protests.
The government’s fears are rooted in the latest wave of protests in Iran, which began on December 28, 2025, and grew into the country’s largest uprising since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Saediniya, a well-known cafe chain with 10 branches in Iran, closed its branches on this day in support of calls for strikes. It was subsequently accused of engaging in “propaganda against the state.”
Iran’s Supreme Court has now upheld the sentence of Sadegh Saedinia, the owner of the cafe chain, to 12 years and six months in prison, along with the confiscation of his assets.
He was arrested over his support for the protests, and all branches of his cafe chain were confiscated and shut down by judicial order.

Other cafes, including “Lamiz” and “Voria,” faced a broadly similar fate. Voria is owned by a prominent Iranian footballer. Both were sealed by judicial order because of their indirect support for calls to protest. Cafe closures have not been confined to periods of protest, however, and the practice continues.
The rise of the cafe culture
Tehran has seen a surge in the number of cafes over the past decade, rising from around 300 in the early 2010s to as many as 4,000 now, according to various estimates.

Some experts attribute the growing number to changes in urban lifestyles in recent years. They see this as more than the expansion of a particular type of business and describe it as a sign of wider social and cultural changes within Iranian society.

“The explosive growth of cafes in society can, to some extent, be seen as a social response to living in a state of chronic crisis,” Saba Alaleh, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst whose work focuses on political and social issues, told DW’s Persian service.
“In such circumstances, people are not simply looking to consume or be entertained. They are looking for a place to temporarily distance themselves from the pressures of everyday life,” she said.

“In this sense, the cafe becomes a third space. It is neither home nor the workplace, but a space between the two where people can briefly step away from their everyday roles and pressures, connect with others, and feel that life is still somewhat manageable and normal.”
The cafe trend has become particularly popular among Gen Z, who are bearing the brunt of runaway inflation and steep living costs in Iran.

“The young people who gather in these cafes do not necessarily come from affluent backgrounds,” Nasser, a cafe owner in Tehran, told DW. “In many parts of Tehran, young people from the middle class also meet at cafes, and many of our customers belong to this group.”
The political role of cafes
Even before the latest bout of nationwide protests that began at the end of last year, shutting down cafes was common practice for the Iranian government.
Most of these crackdowns and closures, however, were carried out under the pretext of enforcing compulsory hijab.
The protests that began in late December 2025 changed that, with cafes becoming the target more often and for varied reasons.
“They shut down our cafe on the pretext that we had served customers who were not wearing the hijab, but that is only an excuse,” Nasser said.
“Outside, on the streets of Tehran, women and girls have effectively abandoned the compulsory hijab, yet the government expects us not to allow them into the cafe,” he added.
Maintaining control over social spaces
Alaleh said the issue is no longer simply about cracking down on women for not wearing the hijab.

“Authoritarian governments generally seek to control the flow of information, social interactions and the organization of citizens,” she pointed out. “Any space beyond the direct supervision of those in power that allows trust, dialogue and social ties to develop can weaken part of the government’s monopoly over the social sphere.”
The expert said the crackdown on cafes and cafegoers is part of the government’s efforts to preserve its monopoly over social spaces.

She underlined that to a security apparatus, even a group of young people casually sitting together can represent the emergence of an independent social network outside the formal structures of power.
“The broader and more deeply rooted these independent networks become, the more difficult it is for the government to maintain exclusive control over the public sphere,” added Alaleh. /dl

articles.title: Trump pledges $5,000 to every adult American if Republicans win November elections
articles.summary: The controversial offer was made in a speech at the party's first-ever convention in the middle of a US presidential term.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump says he would offer every adult American a $5,000 (£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November's midterm elections - a plan that would cost more than a trillion dollars.
The controversial offer was made in a speech at the party's first-ever convention in the middle of a US presidential term.
He gave no details on how the plan would work or where the money would come from - saying only that the money would have to be spent in the US.
Democrats quickly labelled it an "empty promise" and others questioned whether such a pledge was legal.
There are nearly 270 million American adults, which means a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.

Questions about whether his plan was possible have started to be asked - especially as prices rise in the US - partially as a result of the consequences of the war that the US and Israel started with Iran in February.

Iran's retaliation has included attacks against US bases and allies in the Gulf - but crucially it has largely closed the Strait of Hormuz where about a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit.
The blockage has caused fluctuation in oil prices worldwide and Trump has faced pressure from his party to end the war.
On Wednesday, the US president warned his supporters that the war would not end until after the midterms and that oil prices would not come down until then.
He made the comments ahead of his speech in Texas, repeating it at the convention where he argued that short-term economic pain was worth it to prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.

Trump's long speech at the Republican convention in Dallas, Texas, touched at the core of the conflict - the impact on the Americans' standard of living and his pledge to increase their spending power drew raucous applause in the hall.

"If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them," Trump said, "I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000."
"We don't want you going to Canada to spend the money," he said.
"We don't want you going to China, to Germany. You got to spend the money in the United States of America." It is not clear how the spending would be monitored.
It is not the first time that Trump promised such payouts - he has previously proposed $2,000 cheques to be funded by tariff revenues.
Other US politicians in the past have also promised economic rewards in return for electoral success.
For instance, Democrats in Georgia promised $2,000 relief payments if their party took control of the Senate at the height of the Covid-19 pandemic.
In the US, Congress authorises spending and, in his speech in Dallas, the president did not say on whether he planned to ask for such approval for the payments - which he dubbed "Trump Dividends".
However, in addition to the overall cost to the US treasury, the latest offer from the US president may raise legal questions.
Federal laws prohibit payments that are intended to influence voting.
However, some experts say Trump's promise may be seen as a pledge to cut taxes, which is legal.
An election law expert who spoke to the New York Times said Trump's promise would also be covered by the free-speech protection guaranteed under the First Amendment of the US Constitution.

articles.title: DOJ: Manila Interpol to complete docs for Red Notice requests vs Co, others
articles.summary: DOJ Secretary Frederick Visa said other countries should not be a "safe haven" for corrupt officials who are trying to evade accountability.

blocks.text: September 10, 2026 | 2:48pm
Former Rep. Elizaldy Co appeared released a video statement on Nov. 26, 2025.
Zaldy Co / Philstar.com's screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Justice said Thursday, September 10, that Interpol may soon issue Red Notices for former lawmaker Zaldy Co and other fugitives facing charges in the Philippines as authorities work to complete the necessary requirements.

Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida said in a press briefing on Thursday, September 10, that the Philippine Center on Transnational Crimes (PCTC) and Manila Interpol are currently completing the requirements for the requests involving Co and other fugitives from justice.

“Tingin po namin sa lalong madaling panahon, malapit na magkaroon ng kaganapan ‘yung ating kagustuhan na magkaroon ng Red Notice. Hindi lang ho kay former Congressman Zaldy Co, kun’di sa iba pa pong fugitives from justice,” Vida said.
(We think it will be issued soon, our request for the issuance of Red Notice will be realized in the near future. Not only for former Congressman Zaldy Co, but also for other fugitives from justice.)
Among those fugitives, he said, is former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque, who faces anti-trafficking charges related to Philippine offshore gaming operations (POGO).
A Red Notice is an international request for law enforcement agencies to locate and provisionally arrest an individual with a view to extradition.

Earlier this week, Ombudsman Boying Remulla and Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla were reported to have flown to France separately to coordinate with authorities to track Co after the Sandiganbayan issued an arrest warrant against him and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez over their P7.44-billion plunder charge.
Jonvic earlier said he is set to meet with Interpol, which is headquartered in Lyon, France, while Boying is set to talk with French authorities in Paris.
'Not a safe haven'

Vida said the DOJ is also strengthening its cooperation with international agencies to ensure that asylum systems will not be abused by Filipino fugitives, adding that other countries should not be a ‘safe haven’ for officials facing corruption-related charges.
In April, Malacañang confirmed that Co is seeking political asylum in France, while the DOJ said on Thursday in the same press briefing that Roque applied for asylum in Austria.
He said the Philippine government consistently invokes the UN Convention Against Corruption in its coordination with other countries because it is universally accepted.

“‘Yan po ay inuulit-ulit ng iba’t ibang opisyales at kawani ng inyong pamahalaang Pilipinas na, pareho naman tayo dito, ayaw n’yo ng korapsyon, ayaw din namin ng korapsyon. Huwag n’yong payagan na ‘yung sistema o ‘yung option na mag-apply ng asylum ay pamamaraan para makapagtago sa pananagutan,” Vida said.

(That is being repeatedly invoked by different officials and members of your Philippine government, that we are just the same, you dislike corruption, we alos dislike corruptiion. Don't let the system and option of applying for asylum become a way to evade accountability.)
The Philippine government, however, does not oppose asylum applications by fugitives from justice as it only reinforces their requests.

“Kasi kapag nag-oppose ang gobyerno, lalong maha-highlight na ‘uy politically oppressed ‘to’”, Vida said. “Wala naman pong political oppression na nangyayari. Ang gusto lang natin managot sila sa sistemang legal ng Pilipinas.”

(Because if the government opposed, it would be highlighted that ‘this is politically oppressed’. There’s no political oppression happening. What we want is for them to be held liable under Philippine legal systems.)

articles.title: PH seen as attractive, but world remains unconvinced of its capabilities
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is an “attractive brand” but has yet to convince the world of its capabilities, an analysis of the 2026 Best Countries Index showed. The index, developed by WPP…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is an “attractive brand” but has yet to convince the world of its capabilities, an analysis of the 2026 Best Countries Index showed.
The index, developed by WPP BAV, or BrandAsset Valuator, and the Wharton School, placed the Philippines 45th among 85 countries.
It evaluates how people perceive the countries across 73 attributes arranged into 10 dimensions, such as entrepreneurship, agility, cultural influence, openness to business and power.
Switzerland ranked first overall.

blocks.caption: inqmetrics

blocks.text: For Dr. Alicor Panao, Inquirer data scientist and associate professor at the University of the Philippines, the country can be considered an attractive brand that “has yet to convince the world of what it can do.”
RELATED STORY: Philippines trails Southeast Asian peers in good governance index
Across the region, the Philippines ranked last among the six Southeast Asian countries in the index, behind Singapore (12th), Thailand (30th), Malaysia (36th), Indonesia (40th) and Vietnam (41st).

“The gap is even wider with Asia’s leading countries,” Panao said. Japan ranked second, while South Korea placed 13th and China 14th, all performing strongly on attributes associated with economic dynamism, influence and national power.
PH strength, weakness
The Philippines, by contrast, performed better on attributes that make it appealing than on those that signal what it can accomplish, Panao pointed out.
It ranked 27th in adventure and 22nd in the open for business component, but only 50th in entrepreneurship, 47th in agility, 44th in cultural influence and 48th in power.
“That distinction matters because these measures are closely associated with economic performance and national wealth,” he said.
For Panao, the country’s standing probably reflects “a lingering uncertainty about the Philippines as a growth story,” which he described as an ultimate soft-power problem.
“A country’s influence rests not only on what it possesses, but on what others believe it can become,” he said.
Panao said it is not difficult to love the Philippines.
“The challenge is to become not only a country the world likes, but one whose capabilities the world trusts and whose influence it respects.” /dm

articles.title: August of 2026 hottest month ever recorded globally – EU monitor
articles.summary: PARIS — The EU’s climate monitor said Thursday that August was the hottest single month ever recorded globally, with ocean temperatures also reaching unprecedented highs as western Europe…

blocks.text: PARIS — The EU’s climate monitor said Thursday that August was the hottest single month ever recorded globally, with ocean temperatures also reaching unprecedented highs as western Europe capped its warmest summer.
In response to the assessment by the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the UN warned that until humanity weaned off fossil fuels, the planet would only push deeper into uncharted territory.
Copernicus observations go back to 1940 but other evidence — such as ice cores, tree rings and coral skeletons — allow scientists to place today’s climate against a much longer historical context.

“Humans haven’t seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years,” Samantha Burgess from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which oversees Copernicus, told AFP.

Global average air temperatures in August were 16.96C, Copernicus said — surpassing by 0.01C the previous all-time monthly record set in July 2023. Copernicus said it considered the two months joint-highest given the narrow difference.

Scientists say that human activity — primarily the burning of coal, oil and gas — has warmed the planet by roughly 1.4C since pre-industrial times and increased the severity and likelihood of extreme weather.
Yet heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions rose to new highs in 2025.

“The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiraling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling,” United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said of the Copernicus report.
More ahead
Global sea surface temperatures also set a new daily high and tied equal-hottest for August, extending a three-month streak of record-breaking warmth across the world’s oceans.
More than 90 percent of excess heat trapped by greenhouse gas emissions has been absorbed by the oceans, sparing land from warming but at severe cost to marine life, reefs and coastal communities.
Records tumbled in overheated basins like the Atlantic and Mediterranean and also the tropical Pacific, where the strongest El Nino weather pattern in the modern era is fast accumulating strength.
These events are marked by unusually warm Pacific waters but raise the odds of wild weather thousands of miles away, from floods in Peru to droughts in Africa and wildfires in Australia.
The warmer phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino episodes usually deliver a temporary spike in global temperatures already elevated by long-term background warming.

Scientists expect records to keep falling in the months ahead as this “super” El Nino approaches peak intensity around December and for 2027 — and maybe even 2026 — to become the hottest years ever observed.

“Climate change makes every El Nino hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil, and gas these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming,” said Friederike Otto, a climate scientist from Imperial College London.
Sizzling summer
Copernicus also said that August “marked the end of western Europe’s warmest summer” that surpassed the long-standing record set in 2003.
The June to August season was defined by severe, back-to-back heatwaves that shut schools, dried up rivers and primed the land for devastating wildfires.
Between mid-July and mid-August, the continent’s EuroMomo monitoring platform estimated that Europe saw more than 32,000 excess deaths.
Scientists from the World Weather Attribution network concluded that a particularly strong heatwave in June would have been “virtually impossible” without the influence of climate change.
But extraordinary heat was felt around the globe.
On Wednesday, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said the contiguous United States has endured its hottest summer on record.
And regions home to around 900 million people lived through the hottest July ever observed, according to AFP analysis of Copernicus data.

“We’ve had an exceptional summer — not only in Europe, but other parts of the world where records that have existed for close to a century have fallen,” said Burgess, an ocean scientist and strategic lead for at ECMWF.
The climate would “continue to get more extreme unless we turn off the tap to global emissions”, she added. /dl

articles.title: Thailand kindergarten shooting: Suspected gunman surrenders
articles.summary: BANGKOK — A police officer who allegedly gunned down his wife at the kindergarten where she was a teacher in eastern Thailand surrendered Thursday after an overnight standoff with authorities,…

blocks.text: BANGKOK — A police officer who allegedly gunned down his wife at the kindergarten where she was a teacher in eastern Thailand surrendered Thursday after an overnight standoff with authorities, officials said.

Tatsapong Tongthat, an officer at the Bang Lamung station in Chonburi province, allegedly killed his wife late Wednesday morning inside a building at the Nongplalai Municipal Kindergarten about 150 kilometers (93 miles) southeast of the capital Bangkok, according to the provincial government.
Authorities said he fled to his home after the shooting and police surrounded the house, where he remained until surrendering after an 18-hour standoff.

School safety and gun violence in Thailand have come under scrutiny after a 14-year-old opened fire at his high school and family home on Aug. 7, killing eight people and injuring more than 20 before apparently taking his own life.
Another 14-year-old student was arrested Sept. 2 after he fired several shots but failed to injure anyone at his school in Kamphaeng Phet province, 200 kilometers (120 miles) north of Bangkok.

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Asia despite fairly restrictive gun laws. While mass shootings are still rare, Thailand has seen an uptick in high-profile attacks in recent years. /dl

articles.title: Jacqui Lambie calls Pauline Hanson an ‘angry little woman’ after One Nation cartoon calling Andrew Hastie a traitor
articles.summary: Lambie, a veteran and Tasmanian senator, says One Nation leader is a ‘coward’ who is showing her ‘true colours’
articles.byline: Krishani Dhanji, Sarah Basford Canales andTom McIlroy

blocks.text: Jacqui Lambie has escalated her attack on Pauline Hanson, describing her as an “angry little woman” and a “bloody coward” after refusing to apologise or take down a One Nation cartoon labelling Liberal frontbencher and SAS veteran Andrew Hastie a “traitor”.

Lambie, a crossbencher and army veteran herself, defended Hastie on Thursday, after he called on Hanson to take ownership for a One Nation animated cartoon on social media in which he is repeatedly described as a traitor for giving evidence against Victoria Cross recipient Ben Roberts-Smith in his failed defamation case.
Senior Liberals and RSL Australia also joined condemnation of the cartoon on Thursday, with the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, calling for it to be taken down.
Hastie has challenged Hanson and Nationals defector Barnaby Joyce to take responsibility for the One Nation video, promising a costly political battle.
Lambie told ABC radio the cartoon should be immediately taken down and that Hanson was now showing her “true colours”.
“What she’s doing in those cartoons is absolutely disgusting. They are full of bloody violence,” Lambie said.
“But attacking Andrew Hastie, a veteran that has served in our Afghanistan war, or any other veteran, is the lowest ebb you can possibly do. That woman is nothing less than a bloody coward.

“I tell you what, you’re seeing her true colours start to shine now. You watch this, the Australian people. Here comes coward Hanson … And any veteran out there thinking about voting for One Nation or standing for them, I tell you what, you had better think twice.”
Later on Thursday, Lambie joined News24 where she launched an extraordinary tirade against the Queensland senator over her track record on veterans.

“She’s dividing this country. She is dividing it. She’s not uniting it. She’s an angry little woman with so much baggage on her that everybody else and her supporters think that is acceptable behaviour, and think it’s everybody else’s fault besides theirs.”

Hastie is an SAS veteran and served twice in Afghanistan but has attracted the ire of One Nation and Hanson’s billionaire backer, Gina Rinehart, after he gave evidence against Roberts-Smith in a failed defamation case against Nine newspapers.
Hanson and Rinehart say Roberts-Smith is being unfairly targeted over war crimes allegations related to his service between 2009 and 2012.
Hastie on Thursday ruled out legal action against Hanson, due to Rinehart’s backing.
“I think it shows [Hanson] to be weak and glass-jawed. I gave her the opportunity to either own her words publicly or to take it down. She chose neither,” he told ABC radio.
“She’s not fit to govern this country. And she’s also cast a massive slur on veterans around the country who think that Australian soldiers should hold high standards of conduct on the battlefield.

“I’m not after legal action, particularly when she’s financed by Australia’s richest person. Why would I walk into a fight that I can’t win financially? But yes, I’m going to impose costs politically.”

Hanson again claimed she had not personally called Hastie a coward, despite posting the video on her social media accounts. Yesterday she told The Nightly newspaper that she would call Hastie a “wanker” instead.
after newsletter promotion
Taylor also called on Hanson to take down the cartoon during a press conference, and said it was wrong for it to remain online.
“Andrew Hastie has served this country with distinction as an officer in the SAS. She should take it down,” Taylor said.
The opposition leader declined to back Hastie’s description of Hanson as “weak and glass-jawed”.
RSL Australia said calling a veteran a “traitor” was a “slur” and sent a “corrosive message” that “your service can be recast as betrayal the moment it’s politically convenient”.

“This may have begun as a political dispute between Senator Hanson and Mr Hastie, however, when a person’s military service is used as the punchline, when the word ‘traitor’ is thrown at someone who has worn the uniform and deployed on operations, that stops being politics and starts being an attack on every veteran’s service,” the group said.
The Greens senator David Shoebridge also blasted Hanson, telling News24 it was disgraceful to attack the Liberal frontbencher for giving evidence to a trial under oath.

“I disagree with pretty much everything that comes out of Hastie’s mouth, like his whole suite of policies are things that I tend to oppose … but for the life of me, I can’t work out how any political party can stand by an attack on somebody because they go into court and they tell the truth as they understand it,” he said.
“I mean, it’s actually pretty fucking disgraceful to attack him for that.”
James Paterson, the shadow defence minister, said Hanson and her strategist James Ashby “should be ashamed of themselves”.
“I would never dream of accusing someone who has served in uniform for our country of being a traitor,” he said.

“There’s no graver accusation to make, particularly about someone like Andrew Hastie. Andrew Hastie signed up to the ADF after 9/11. He signed up to fight Islamist terrorists as part of the global war on terror. He served on the frontlines in Afghanistan over multiple tours. What service has anyone in One Nation given that compares in any way, shape or form to Andrew Hastie’s service?”

articles.title: Sydney man jailed for 3.5 years over ‘fake’ defence reports for Chinese spies
articles.summary:
Alexander Csergo, 58, sentenced over reckless foreign interference after preparing documents for duo who approached on LinkedIn

A seemingly innocuous message on a social media platform has…

blocks.text: A seemingly innocuous message on a social media platform has snowballed into a Sydney man being jailed for foreign interference.
Alexander Csergo, 58, was jailed for three years and six months on Thursday, after being found guilty by a jury in March of helping Chinese spies.
With time served, he will be eligible for parole in October.

Between May and December 2022, the business owner knew he was assisting Chinese operatives – known only as Ken and Evelyn – when he prepared fake, plagiarised reports about Australia’s defence arrangements, New South Wales district court judge Craig Smith said on Thursday.
His relationship with the pair began after the Australian IT consultant was approached on LinkedIn by a woman claiming to be from a Chinese thinktank in November 2021.
Csergo, who was living and working in China at the time, should have known Ken and Evelyn were working for China’s Ministry of State Security, his trial had heard.
But Smith found it was not proven that Csergo was reckless about the prospect of helping the foreign power from the moment he read the message.
“Spotting Chinese intelligence operatives on that program requires training on what to look for,” the judge said.

The 58-year-old Australian used open-source information to compile reports on a variety of topics, including lithium mining, German politics, defence and security. He was specifically asked to dig up private information about Australia’s involvement in the Quad security group and the AUKUS deal, Smith said.
He also falsely claimed he had interviewed a number of individuals, including former prime minister and Mandarin speaker Kevin Rudd, his trial had heard.
The reports were handed to Ken or Evelyn in person – sometimes at restaurants and cafes devoid of other people – in exchange for envelopes containing the equivalent of thousands of dollars in cash.
While the information was worthless, the jury accepted prosecution submissions that the relationship with Csergo and his contacts was valuable.
after newsletter promotion
“I do not consider what he did can be described as overly sophisticated,” Smith said.
“But there was certainly a degree of sophistication around the extensive nature of what he did.”

Ken also handed Csergo a “shopping list” of sensitive topics to research when he returned to Australia in early 2023. However, the judge said there was no evidence Csergo carried out any espionage relating to the list.
Ultimately, Smith ruled it was important to deter the wider community from being wooed into compromising Australia’s national security.

articles.title: Labor friends of Palestine criticise Australia’s decision not to join sanctions on Israeli settlements in West Bank
articles.summary:
Australia declined to join move by UK, Canada and France in banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements

Labor party members have criticised the federal government for not following the…

blocks.text: Labor party members have criticised the federal government for not following the UK, Canada and France in banning trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, urging Penny Wong to mount a stronger response to violence against Palestinians.

The Labor Friends of Palestine group wrote to the foreign minister on Wednesday, calling for Australia to join a coordinated approach with allies and partners overseas, in line with changes to the party’s national platform agreed in July.

A campaign group within the party’s rank and file membership, Labor Friends of Palestine called for careful policy design, rather than “inaction,” including on how targeted trade restrictions could be implemented while protecting Palestinian workers and avoiding unintended consequences.
This week, Wong confirmed Australia was preparing another round of sanctions against Israel, but stopped short of joining the UK in banning trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, called efforts by Israel to control the territory unlawful and agreed there was “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists”.
Convenors of the group told Wong joining the new push led by the UK would be consistent with the principles endorsed by Labor members at the party’s national conference in Adelaide.
Labor’s platform, which is used to guide policy development, opposes the annexation of Palestinian territory and calls for Israel to bring illegal settlement activity and the occupation to an end.
It calls on the government to end any support being given to illegal settlement activity or extremist violence, and to implement further action and sanctions as necessary.

“The announcement by Canada, France and the United Kingdom provides Australia with an opportunity to give practical effect to those commitments,” the group said in a letter to Wong and provided to Guardian Australia.

“Australia has already worked alongside these countries in responding to escalating settler violence. In June, Australia joined Canada, France, Norway and the United Kingdom in coordinated sanctions and other measures against extremist settlers and those supporting violence against Palestinian civilians.”

The UK will ban goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories, and introduce a new ban on arms licences and other exports. Sanctions against individuals are also planned but the plan could take six to nine months to be implemented.

In a joint statement, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, said they were taking further action to push for progress on a two-state solution.
Nine European countries also said they were considering similar measures.
While Australia has previously acted in concert with partners overseas, Wong said this week Australia was not currently pushing for a broad ban on goods produced in Israeli settlements.
She told the Senate on Thursday claims by the Greens that Australia was trying to placate the Netanyahu government were wrong.
“I think the Prime Minister Netanyahu’s government has made very, very clear their displeasure at the actions that the Albanese government has taken,” she said.
Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi challenged Wong to say if she agreed with Miliband that ethnic cleansing of Palestinians was taking place in the West Bank.
Instead Wong said Australia had “sanctioned Israeli extremists for the abhorrent settler violence terrorising Palestinian communities.”

Wong has been working with the family of the killed Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom on a response to the Israel Defense Forces’ decision not to open a criminal investigation into Gaza strikes that killed her and six of her colleagues.

articles.title: Senate panel approves PH-France Status of Visiting Forces Agreement
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The Senate committee on foreign relations on Thursday approved the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOFVA) between the Philippines and France. The SOVFA between the two…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Senate committee on foreign relations on Thursday approved the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOFVA) between the Philippines and France.
The SOVFA between the two countries was signed on March 26, 2026 – marking the first SOVFA agreement between the Philippines and a European country.
A SOVFA allows nations to have joint military exercises, intelligence sharing, and humanitarian relief operations.
So far, the Philippines has SOVFAs with Canada, New Zealand, the United States, Japan, and Australia.
Negotiations for a SOVFA between the Philippines and the United Kingdom are also underway.
Invited as a resource person in the hearing was Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. who highlighted the strategic importance of the partnership with France.
Teodoro first highlighted France’s position on international law.

“Its interest in freedom of navigation and other principles enshrined under UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea) is also very important and critical to them… France calls on the application of international norms, the UN Charter, the UNCLOS, without reservation,” Teodoro said.
“They fully support the arbitral award that the Philippines won,” he added.

Teodoro pointed out that as a first SOVFA with France, both as a European country and as a country with several territories in the Pacific region, would expand the Philippines connections with such regions.

“Our partnership with France is merely an offshoot of country-to-country partnership. Nonetheless it gives a toehold to the interconnectivity between the Mediterranean Seas, and the other seas, the Persian Gulf, and the greater Indo-Pacific as a whole,” Teodoro stated.
This, he said, would be important for the territorial stress experienced by the Philippines as the Indo-Pacific is known to support the rules-based international order.

“For the Philippines, we view it as a matter of no choice, because our territory is under severe stress, to put it politely, by the unilateral and illegal acts of China. Thus, we cannot deny the fact that as many coalition partners we have, it adds to our deterrent posture of our country,” he explained.
Department of Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary Edgar Badajos expressed support for the treaty, likewise noting the SOVFA’s importance to cooperation in security and defense.
Badajos further pointed out the benefit of such partnership to a smaller country.

“These targeted diplomatic frameworks enable smaller states like the Philippines, to give real substance to international law especially in a geopolitically critical region and constantly challenging defense and security landscape,” he said.
He also remarked that partnerships with different countries is the Philippines’ way of exercising its diplomatic independence.

With overwhelming support from the executive departments, foreign relations panel chairperson Sen. Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri vowed to present the committee report to the plenary by September 14, in hopes of passing the measure on second and third reading. /gsg

articles.title: Singapore says Iran-backed militia commander sought to enter city-state
articles.summary: SINGAPORE — A commander of an Iran-backed Iraqi militia who allegedly plotted attacks against Jewish targets in Europe, Canada and the United States tried to enter Singapore on multiple…

blocks.text: SINGAPORE — A commander of an Iran-backed Iraqi militia who allegedly plotted attacks against Jewish targets in Europe, Canada and the United States tried to enter Singapore on multiple occasions, the city-state’s security agency said Thursday.

Singapore said it would not have allowed Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi to enter the country, but warned the case highlighted how conflicts in the Middle East could raise terrorism risks in Southeast Asia.
In an annual terrorism threat assessment report, the Internal Security Department (ISD) said that Al-Saadi, who is in US custody awaiting trial, applied for visas to visit Singapore in 2023 and 2024.
“Baqer had applied for visas to visit Singapore on three separate occasions in 2023 and 2024, but did not eventually travel to Singapore,” the agency said.
The ISD said it believed Al-Saadi had travelled elsewhere in Southeast Asia during that period.
“Had he attempted to enter Singapore, he would have been denied entry,” it added.

“We do not discount the possibility that Baqer’s travel to this region could have been for terrorism purposes, and he could have set his sights on targeting Singapore, including US and Israeli/Jewish interests here.”
The agency said it was working with intelligence partners to investigate his activities.
The ISD cited the case as an example of how overseas conflicts “have heightened the threat of attack against Singapore” and Southeast Asia.
Singapore and the region “continue to feel the ripple effects of the geopolitical tensions and instability in the Middle East,” it said.

Activities by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and its network of armed proxies “have elevated the threat of terrorism beyond the immediate theatre of conflict in the Middle East,” it added.
US prosecutors identified Al-Saadi in charges filed in May as a senior figure in Kataeb Hezbollah, an Iraqi armed group designated by Washington as a terrorist organisation linked to the IRGC.
According to US authorities, he directed and encouraged attacks on US and Israeli interests, and urged the killing of Americans and Jews in retaliation for the war against Iran.
He was arrested in Turkey before being transferred to the United States, where he remains in custody awaiting trial.
Kataeb Hezbollah has denied that Al-Saadi is a member of the group.
Southeast Asia has been a target of militant attacks in the past, including the 2002 nightclub bombings in the Indonesian resort island of Bali that killed 202 people. /dl

articles.title: Thursday briefing: 68 facts about the Bayeux tapestry as it goes on display
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: No Bayeux ticket? Everything you need to know about the sold-out exhibition – from its epic journey to London to a Game of Thrones likeness

Good morning. If you live…

blocks.text: Good morning. If you live in the UK, you have probably heard about the Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which opens today, and you probably haven’t got a ticket. The digital queue was nine-hours long when they first went on sale in July, and the exhibition has already broken the British Museum’s record for the number of tickets sold in a single day.

Some lucky individuals, including King Charles and aspiring overlord Peter Thiel, have been treated to early previews of the medieval tapestry. Guests staying at One Aldwych, a hotel where rooms go for £1,000 a night, can partake in the “Bayeux experience” with a themed cocktail (mead spritzer, anyone?), a full English breakfast and preferential access to tickets.

In a break from our regular programming, this morning’s newsletter brings you 68 facts about the Bayeux tapestry for anyone who hasn’t been able to see the real thing. That’s one fact for each of its 68 metres (bonus fact: it’s 68.3m long). If that’s not your vibe, just be glad I didn’t manage to find 1,066 facts. First, here are the headlines.
Five big stories

items: Reform | The Met police will investigate allegations that Reform UK broke electoral law relating to overseas donations as part of a wider inquiry.
UK- Israel | Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end.

Technology | Just a day after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, US politicians have begun lashing out about the risks of the burgeoning technology.
UK news | Protesters who gathered outside a Portsmouth hotel mistook Pakistan’s under-19 cricket team for asylum seekers.

US news | Donald Trump pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections, during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

blocks.text: In depth: From nudity, a save from the Nazis and its restoration, a buffet of Bayeux facts

blocks.caption: Children look at a section of the Bayeux tapestry depicting King Harold’s death during a preview at the British Museum in London. Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/Reuters

blocks.text: 1. First of all, as the exhibition’s curator Michael Lewis points out in his book, the Bayeux tapestry isn’t really a tapestry. It’s “more accurately described as an embroidery”, Lewis writes. (Nobody actually calls it an embroidery, though, so we’ll stick with tapestry).
2. The embroidery tapestry tells the story of the events that culminated in the Battle of Hastings in 1066, when William the Conquerer defeated King Harold.

3. It was supposedly commissioned by Bishop Odo, William the Conquerer’s half-brother, for his newly built cathedral in Bayeux in 1077. He was prone to “self-aggrandisement” (in Lewis’s words), which is why he gave himself a starring role in the tapestry.
4. But it wasn’t made in Bayeux. Researchers think it was probably made in England, near Canterbury.
5. It’s embroidered on linen, with 10 colours of woollen thread likely dyed with woad, madder and indigo.
6. Its nine panels were embroidered separately, and then stitched together to form a continuous picture.
7. It features 623 men, 190 horses, 35 dogs, 37 buildings (including Mont-Saint-Michel) and 41 ships.
8. It may have had a single master designer who plotted its narrative, but …
9. The embroidery was almost certainly stitched by multiple women (William of Poitiers cited English women as skilled embroiderers).
10. It’s unclear how long it took them – one estimate reckons the stitching took between two and four years.

11. Yet, only three women actually feature in the tapestry. None of them are having a good time: one is weeping at her husband’s deathbed, another is fleeing a burning building and a third is being assaulted by a priest.

12. This third figure is Ælfgyva (meaning elf-gift), the only named woman in the tapestry. Scholars think that she could be Emma of Normandy, who was accused of having an affair with the Bishop of Winchester.
13. The tapestry conveniently doesn’t mention Edgar Ætheling, who had a stronger hereditary claim to the English throne in 1066 than either William or Harold.
14. The borders tell their own stories. They’re filled with fantastical beasts, creating what the Guardian’s art critic Jonathan Jones described as a “marginal world of monsters and myths”.
15. The upper border features one of the first depictions of Haley’s Comet.

16. The tapestry also shows a figure with the name Harold, depicting the famous (and probably apocryphal) moment he was struck in the eye by an arrow. Most scholars think Harold was actually hacked to death.
17. It was possibly designed to be interpreted by a live storyteller in front of an audience, much like an epic poem.
18. It’s damaged at the end, and incomplete. Nobody knows what scene would have finished the tapestry (some think it could have been a depiction of William’s coronation at Westminster Abbey in 1066).
19. It survived at least three fires in Bayeux Cathedral.

20. The first recorded reference to the tapestry was in the 1476 inventory of Bayeux cathedral, which described a “very long and narrow hanging of linen, embroidered with figures and inscriptions representing the Conquest of England.”

blocks.caption: Museum staff work on the unveiling of the Bayeux tapestry. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: 21. The tapestry hasn’t always been well looked after. For centuries it was rolled out for cathedral visitors. One visiting English antiquary observed in the early 1800s that it was “much rubbed at the beginning, torn towards the end.”
22. In 1792, during the French Revolution, the tapestry was nearly used to cover a wagon (it was saved at the last minute by an official who swapped it for a piece of canvas).
23. In 1794, an proposal was briefly floated to cut the tapestry into strips to decorate a festival float.
24. A 19th-century British artist secretly snipped off two fragments that ended up in a London museum (these were eventually returned to Bayeux).
25. In 1803, Napoleon had the tapestry temporarily moved from Bayeux to Paris, where it hung on display at the Louvre, to rally support for his planned invasion of Britain.
26. The first full photographic copy of the tapestry was made for the South Kensington Museum in 1872 (now the V&A museum).
27. A group of women in Staffordshire created the largest Bayeux reproduction in 1885, which is displayed in Reading Museum. It took them 18 months.
28. They removed 93 penises from their reproduction, 88 belonging to horses and five to men.
29. The Nazis saw the tapestry as a propaganda tool, and wanted to establish that Normans were actually the descendants of Viking settlers.
30. They appointed a professor of Viking archaeology as the leader of “Special Assignment Bayeaux” to study it.
31. Heinrich Himmler tasked two SS officers in 1944 to seize the Bayeaux tapestry from the basement of the Louvre, where it was being stored.
32. A group of local resistance fighters tipped off by code breakers at Bletchley Park managed to intercept the officers and protect the tapestry.
33. Since 1983, the tapestry has been displayed at the Bayeux museum, in a 17th-century seminary near Bayeux’s medieval town centre.
34. When the tapestry arrived at the Bayeux museum in the 1980s, photos show that it appeared to have been folded and hoisted up a stairwell.
35. It’s incredibly fragile, and liable to fray. A 2020 study found the tapestry had “24,204 stains, 16,445 wrinkles, 9,646 gaps in the cloth or the embroidery” and “30 non-stabilised tears.”
36. The first request for the Bayeux tapestry to be loaned to Britain was in 1953, for Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation. The French refused.
37. Another request was made in 1966, to mark the 900th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings. The French refused, again.

38. In 2013, a committee was formed to advise on how the tapestry could be redisplayed. It raised the prospect of a loan to the UK (“I did sort of bang on about it,” Lewis, a committee member, later recalled, “until I was a bit like a broken record”).
39. The Bayeux museum was scheduled to be closed for refurbishment, creating an opportunity for the tapestry to travel on loan.

40. In January 2018, Emmanuel Macron announced at a summit with Theresa May that the French had agreed to loan the tapestry. Although France had “found the best experts of the world to explain in perfect detail” why the loan “was impossible”, Macron said that the French government had “decided” otherwise.

blocks.caption: French president Emmanuel Macron, King Charles, Queen Camilla and prime minister Andy Burnham view the Bayeux tapestry Exhibition at the British Museum in London. Photograph: Adrian Dennis/PA

blocks.text: 41. Many people insist it should never have been moved. Arts journalist Didier Rykner started a petition against the loan that gained more than 70,000 signatures.
42. The late David Hockney agreed, described the loan as “madness,” and said “some things are too precious to take a risk with.”
43. And two expert reports in 2021 and 2022 advised Macron against the transportation of the tapestry.
44. The loan specified the tapestry had to be stored lying flat, and couldn’t be subject to tremors any greater than two millimetres per second during its transportation.

45. A team of conservators and experts, including a German vibration technology scientist, were involved with its relocation. They designed a meticulous solution for transporting the tapestry involving a “paravent”, a hinged folding screen on wheels.
46. The paravent was designed so it could be closed into a rectangular block with the tapestry inside, effectively folded 28 times.
after newsletter promotion
47. It took ninety people in blue latex gloves seven hours working to extract the tapestry from its case and transfer it to the paravent.

48. It then had to be stored in a specially manufactured crate for shipping. The art logistics firm Hizikia built two nesting crates, with an outer aluminium crate designed to reduce the impact of movement.
49. The firm also provided a customised reinforced truck to dampen vibrations.
50. Experts carried out two dry runs, one with a replica tapestry transported across the channel that made its way to an art warehouse in south London.
51. Data from these dry-runs showed that French roads are smoother than British roads.

52. The tapestry has been insured by the Treasury’s indemnity scheme for £800m, which is more than twice the value of the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction (Salvator Mundi, a painting of Jesus attributed to Leonardo da Vinci).
53. Two threads were reportedly broken when the tapestry arrived in London.
54. At the British Museum, it will be housed in a custom-made case, believed to be the longest ever constructed, and will be exposed to a limited number of light hours per day.
55. When the lights are switched on, they’ll be dimmed to 50 lux, the international museum standard for sensitive materials.
56. Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and King Charles viewed the tapestry last Wednesday.
57. It will be displayed at the British Museum until July 2027, before it returns to a newly built museum in Normandy that will open later next year.
58. Nicholas Cullinan, director of the British Museum, has said he hopes the Bayeux loan could revive the prospect for a loan of the Parthenon marbles.
59. The tapestry has inspired numerous copycats, including the Bloody Sunday Tapestry created by the artist Darren Cullen in 2013.
60. There’s also a Game of Thrones Tapestry at the Ulster Museum in Ireland.

61. The Sun newspaper commissioned a “Bye-EU” tapestry in 2018 to commemorate the Brexit vote, which depicted Boris Johnson in chain mail and Theresa May surrounded by the decapitated corpses of Brussels bureaucrats.
62. A helmet from Sutton Hoo, and the Lewis chess pieces, were both loaned to Normandy museums as part of the Bayeux loan.

63. My favourite bit of any trip to the British Museum is the gift shop (eds: does this count as a fact?), where you can now buy a replica Norman helmet and bottle of Bayeux mead with your Tutankhamun pencil tin.
64. Speaking of Bayeux tat, Nigel Farage sported a Bayeux-themed tie during the 2014 Rochester byelection, a reminder of “the last time we were invaded and taken over”.
65. Radio 4 has devoted a special day of broadcasts to mark the arrival of the tapestry.
66. And the museum’s videos about the tapestry’s arrival are narrated by the Traitors presenter Claudia Winkleman.
67. Philippe Bélavel, Macron’s former culture adviser, has said “such a loan will only happen once and never again.”

articles.title: August hottest month ever recorded, says EU monitor
articles.summary: The average global temperature in August broke the previous record set in 2023. Climate scientists say record summer heat in the northern hemisphere and warmer oceans are all part of a new normal.

image.caption: Summer 2026 scorched Europe with record-breaking heat, drought, and wildfiresImage: Patricia Huchot-Boissier/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

blocks.text: Data from the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service released Thursday showed the average global air temperature last month measured 16.96° Celsius (62.53° F), the highest monthly global average ever recorded.

"Humans haven't seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years," Samantha Burgess from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which oversees Copernicus, told AFP.
Copernicus data, which goes back to 1940, recorded the previous all-time monthly high only three years ago in July 2023.
Western Europe records hottest summer
Western Europe recorded its hottest summer on record this year after successive heatwaves, droughts and wildfires.
Between mid-July and mid-August, Europe saw more than 32,000 excess deaths related to heat, according to estimates from the EuroMomo monitoring platform.
Additionally, ocean temperatures also tied their record high, which extended a three-month streak of record-breaking warmth across the world's oceans.
These warm ocean temperatures come at severe cost to marine life, reefs and coastal communities.

Added to this, what is estimated to be the strongest El Nino in the modern era is set to bring unusually warm Pacific waters, raising the odds of extreme weather across the world, from floods to droughts and wildfires.
Wildfires spread beyond Europe's traditional fire zones
Scientists point to climate change
Scientists primarily attributed the extreme heat primarily to human-caused climate change.

"The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiraling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said in response to the Copernicus report.
Stiell said "until humanity stops burning" coal, oil and gas, extreme heat would continue to break records.

blocks.caption: The world's oceans outside of the polar regions also recorded their joint-highest sea surface temperature for any month on recordImage: HPIC/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Long-term warming currently averages at about 1.4°C higher than pre-industrial levels, just under the 1.5°C limit envisioned under the Paris Agreement.
Last week, the UN said the 1.5°C goal was no longer achievable and urged faster greenhouse gas cuts.

"It is now time to stop acting surprised that our warming planet keeps getting warmer. This is occurring exactly as forecast by scientists literally decades ago," Texas A&M University climate scientist Andrew Dessler told the Associated Press.
"The interesting question is not whether we will keep breaking heat records (we will), but whether we're going to do anything about it or just stand there while the climate train runs us over."
El Nino, regional wars fuel global food crisis

articles.title: Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role
articles.summary:
Dow Jones convicted of one count of deterring Selina Cheng from role at Hong Kong Journalist Association but cleared of second charge

A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of the…

blocks.text: A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of the Wall Street Journal of deterring a reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city.

The newspaper dismissed Selina Cheng just weeks after she was appointed chair of the Hong Kong Journalist Association (HKJA) in 2024. She was told at the time her termination was officially due to restructuring.

Outside court on Thursday, Cheng said: “If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters.”

Principal magistrate David Cheung ruled that Dow Jones Publishing, the parent company of the Wall Street journal, was guilty of “preventing or deterring an employee from exercising trade union rights,” but acquitted it of “dismissing or discriminating against an employee because she exercised those rights.”

Cheng, who covered China’s automobiles and energy sectors for the WSJ, said her editor had told her that employees should not be seen as advocating for press freedom in “places like Hong Kong”, saying it could be perceived as a conflict of interest. She alleged her employer had attempted to prevent her from taking up a role in the union.
She said the company told her that she needed to seek the firm’s approval for outside activities and requested her to leave her then-board position at the association.
Cheng launched the private prosecution against Dow Jones Publishing after losing her job in July 2024, weeks after taking up the position as chair of the union.
The company pleaded not guilty to both charges, which each carry a maximum fine of HK$100,000 (about $12,750).
Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date.

During the trial, the defence argued that Cheng was terminated because of redundancy and that the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that the firm’s management instructed Cheng’s supervisor. The defence also accused Cheng of acting in bad faith in a previous hearing.

But magistrate David Cheung said that Cheng’s termination “was motivated by wrongful and unjustified application of their code of conduct” when it insisted Cheng needed to seek prior approval to stand as chair of HKJA.
Cheung said he accepted Cheng’s explanation, describing the former WSJ reporter as “honest and reliable”, adding she and was clearly motivated by “the wish to see justice”.

Cheng’s termination alarmed journalists, who are already operating in an increasingly restricted media environment in the city, where foreign outlets have traditionally faced less pressure than local news outlets.

“The WSJ set a very bad precedent by punishing an employee who was exercising her constitutionally protected rights in Hong Kong,” said Eric Lai, a senior fellow at the Georgetown Center for Asian Law.

The WSJ maintained there was no link between Cheng’s role in the Hong Kong union and her termination. At the time of Cheng’s dismissal, it issued a statement saying: “The Wall Street Journal has been and continues to be a fierce and vocal advocate for press freedom in Hong Kong and around the world.”

HKJA is the oldest journalist union in Hong Kong. It was established in 1968 and is registered as a trade union representing journalists and workers in news. It has faced increasing pressure since the introduction of a Beijing-imposed national security law in 2020.

Hong Kong has fallen sharply in global press freedom rankings since the law’s introduction. In 2019 Reporters Without Borders ranked the city 73rd in the world. By 2026 it had fallen 67 places to 140th out of 180 countries and territories.

articles.title: Australia: Rising sea levels threaten more than 267,000 properties
articles.summary: BRISBANE — More than 267,000 Australian properties and two million hectares of land could be damaged or lost to rising sea levels and coastal flooding, in a trend that could cost the nation…

blocks.text: BRISBANE — More than 267,000 Australian properties and two million hectares of land could be damaged or lost to rising sea levels and coastal flooding, in a trend that could cost the nation $855 billion.

Western Australia faces the greatest economic losses by 2100 at $230.5 billion, while Queensland has the most properties at risk, with more than 93,000 on the line, followed by NSW with more than 71,000.
The Climate Council issued the warning on Thursday in a report estimating the financial cost of rising sea levels and storm surges, drawing on research from the University of Melbourne.

It comes one week after the United Nations warned the world would exceed 1.5 degrees of warming within years, increasing the risk of sea-level rises and more frequent extreme weather events such as heatwaves, cyclones, floods and fires.
The council’s report, Rising Seas, Rising Bills, estimated the risk of sea-level rises in Australia in an intermediate scenario where global emissions peaked in 2040 and declined rapidly.

It found Australia could suffer $274.3 billion in property losses by 2100 because of inundation of low-lying areas, coastal flooding and land erosion, with effects felt in every state and the Northern Territory.

Damage to land could cost $580.7 billion, with more than 619,000 hectares of farmland at risk, along with more than 379,000 hectares of parks and recreation areas, and more than 23,000 hectares of land hosting critical infrastructure.
Scientists predicted sea levels would rise by at least another 14 centimeters by 2050, Climate Council spokesman Andrew Watkins said, but the actual figure could be higher and the risks greater.

“These are big, big numbers that we need to consider and the economic part of the study is conservative in that it doesn’t account for everything that could happen but for the basic land, property and infrastructure costs,” he told AAP.
“What we want is for people to realise what is at stake here.”
Western Australia, with the biggest coastline, faced the biggest risk of economic loss with more than 586,000 hectares of land exposed to rising seas and storm surges.

But Queensland had the highest number of properties at risk, the report said, with the Gold Coast named the most exposed urban area in Australia, facing the loss of more than 32,000 properties and $84 billion.
Private insurance rarely covered “actions of the sea”, the report noted, and could leave residents with high damage bills.

The federal government should stop approving fossil fuel projects and strengthen emission cuts to avert further risks, Mr Watkins said, but should also work with state and local governments to prevent construction in at-risk areas and preserve coastal regions.
“It is a creeping problem that’s not as obvious as fire and floods and you don’t want to suddenly, too late, realise what the impacts might be,” he said.
“We need to plan now and the sooner we get on to it, the better.”
Rising sea levels were already affecting agriculture in Australia, cane farmer Robert Quirk said.
His land in NSW’s Tweed Valley sits half a meter above sea level, and rising tides mean he has to run pumps throughout the year to drain the fields.
“We have a drainage problem and for every centimetre the ocean rises, I pump another 10 Olympic swimming pools off the farm every rain event,” he said.
“I’ve got little grandchildren who’ll be alive in 2100 and what will they do?” /dl
