articles.title: 'Negative na': Small Manila businesses cut staff, take loans over steep garbage fees
articles.summary: One to two trash bags a day, P60,000 garbage bill: Manila businesses are crying foul over new garbage fees.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Small business owners in Manila are reeling from a sharp increase in garbage collection fees imposed during this year's business permit renewal.

Already struggling with operating costs, business owners interviewed by Philstar.com said the higher fees have pushed their finances further into the red, forcing some to cut staff or take out loans. At least one establishment was also ordered closed by the Manila local government over unpaid permit-related fees.
For Vince Canlas, owner of El Latte Cafe on Taft Avenue, the new fees have made the reality of doing business in Manila an uphill battle.
Originally starting as a milk tea shop in Olongapo, the business relocated to Manila to tap into the large student market near major universities.
The 100-square-meter cafe has just five employees. So when he renewed the permit, he was shocked at what he was asked to pay.
"Nagulat kami sa garbage fee. Na sobrang laki. Nakakagulat lang talaga. Hindi namin in-expect na mangyayari pala sa amin," Canlas told Philstar.com in an interview.
(We were taken aback by how high the garbage fee was. It was really surprising. We never expected this would happen to us.)
Canlas said the cafe incurred nearly P107,000 in fees for its business permit renewal. Around P60,000 was for garbage collection, including interest due to late payment.
"Sabi ko manager ko, 'Sir, gaano ba karami ang tinatapon natin daily?' Sabi niya, 'Boss, ano lang 'to, nasa one to two bags lang.' Sobrang baba so hindi talaga makatarungan ang P60,000," Canlas said.
(I asked my manager how much garbage we generate daily, and he said it was only around one or two bags. Given how little waste we produce, a P60,000 garbage fee is simply unreasonable.)
To survive, Canlas reduced his employees' working days, resulting in lower take-home pay.
"Wala kaming choice kasi wala naman kaming ibang pwedeng i-cut na ano eh. Para lang mabawasan 'yung alam mo 'yun, 'yung gastusin eh," Canlas said.
(We had no choice because there really wasn't anything else we could cut. We just needed to bring down our expenses.)
Making things worse, the Manila local government ordered the closure of his cafe on September 1 after he struggled to settle the fees.
To save the cafe, Canlas took out a new loan to pay the nearly P107,000 assessment on the same day.
After settling the amount, howver, Canlas said the city still required them to pay another P6,200 in penalties before they were allowed to reopen.
"Baka tapusin na lang itong year na 'to. Isara na lang namin ang cafe; wala na talaga eh, negative na dahil sa mga bills," Canlas said.
(We might just finish out this year and shut down the cafe. We really have no choice left. We're already operating at a loss because of all these bills.)
"Grabe, nakaka-iyak sa Manila. Parang tingin nila pinupulot namin ang pera," he added.
Reduced staff
Outdoor seating next to food stalls at Manila's Fusion Alley in Sampaloc as seen in September 2026.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui
For Kriska Castillejos, owner of a food stall near Manila's Fusion Alley in Sampaloc, the financial pressure meant letting go of nine of her 15 employees.
Like other business owners interviewed by Philstar.com, Castillejos said her stall suffered financially because of what she described as a sudden spike in costs of business in the city.
For the previous year, she paid about P14,000 in renewal fees. In 2026, the amount ballooned to P64,000.
"Malaki 'yung ano niya, 'yung impact niya talaga. Lalo na kami maliliit, nagpapasahod kami ng tao," Castillejos said in a Philstar.com interview.
(It really has a huge impact, especially on small business owners like us who have employees to pay.)
The ordinance
In January 2026, the Manila local government began implementing revised garbage collection fees under Ordinance 9151, with some commercial rates rising to 12 times their previous levels.
Before the revised schedule, Manila followed the garbage collection rates under its 2013 Omnibus Revenue Code.
For instance, the quarterly garbage fee for the main office of a commercial bank was previously P1,250, while each branch was charged P225.
Under the revised schedule, both a commercial bank's main office and each branch are charged P15,000 per quarter.
Public eating places with an aggregate area of 100 to less than 200 square meters, meanwhile, are now charged P16,800 per quarter.
Call for fairer fees
Business owners urged Manila Mayor Isko Moreno Domagoso to reconsider the steep increases.
Canlas said he does not hold any personal animosity toward the local government but believes its current policies are putting more pressure on small enterprises.
"Sana ma-hear kami na magiging balance lang sa lahat. May proyekto para sa mahirap, may proyekto para sa mga small business owners," Canlas said.
(I hope we are heard and that there will be balance for everyone, with projects for the poor as well as projects for small business owners.)

"Hindi naman namin hinihiling na malaki ang bumalik sa amin. Ang gusto lang talaga namin makapag-operate nang wala kaming iniisip na, hala, may bayarin malaking ganito. Mabubuhay, makakapag-operate pa ba tayo para sa mga employees natin?" he added.
(We aren't asking for huge returns. All we really want is to operate without constantly worrying about massive bills and wondering whether we can survive and continue operating for our employees.)

Castillejos, meanwhile, urged the city hall to focus on strict waste segregation, penalties for littering and investments in recycling rather than imposing increasingly heavy fees on already struggling businesses.
"Kasi talagang may basura naman tayo eh. Kailangan nating magbayad para sa ika-uunlad din natin. Ang ano ko lang is dapat hindi sobrang taas," Castillejos said.
(We recognize that we generate waste and need to pay our share. My only point is that the fee should not be this high.)
Comparison with other cities
Under Manila's revised schedule, public eating places with an aggregate area of 100 to less than 200 square meters are assessed a quarterly garbage fee of P16,800, or P67,200 annually.
The amount is notably higher than waste collection fees described by other local governments in responses to Philstar.com:

items: San Juan City: Annual garbage fees range from P200 to P15,000 depending on the size and type of business and are collected during the application or renewal of business permits, according to San Juan Mayor Francis Zamora.

Marikina City: Restaurants are charged annual garbage fees of around P3,000 to P5,000, while catering services are charged P12,000 per year. Rates for smaller establishments vary depending on their classification.
Las Piñas: Businesses are charged annual fees ranging from P3,000 to P20,000.
Pasig City: Restaurants and cafes are charged P5 per square meter monthly. For a 100-square-meter cafe, this amounts to P500 a month, or P6,000 annually.
Navotas City: The Assessment Department of Business Permits and Licensing told Philstar.com that the city collects P1,500 to P7,500 as garbage disposal fees for food businesses' annual payments.

blocks.text: What did the Manila LGU say?
Philstar.com has reached out to the Manila Public Information Office for comment but has yet to receive a response as of press time.
In a January statement, the Manila local government defended Ordinance No. 9151 as "lawful and constitutionally sound."

City officials said an earlier Supreme Court ruling involving Quezon City's garbage fees did not apply to Manila's ordinance because the city's revised charges were imposed on businesses as regulatory fees rather than as taxes.

"In contrast, he said, Manila's revised garbage collection fees apply exclusively to business establishments and are imposed as regulatory fees, not taxes, consistent with jurisprudence recognizing the validity of cost-based garbage charges," the Manila LGU's January statement read.

City Legal Officer Luch Gempis Jr. said the rates had not been updated since 2013 despite increases in commercial waste volumes and garbage hauling costs, particularly after Manila was advised to redirect its waste to the New San Mateo Sanitary Landfill in Rizal.
City Treasurer Paul Vega similarly said the revised rates were intended to narrow the gap between the cost of garbage collection and the revenue generated from the fees.

Bureau of Permits Director Levi Facundo, meanwhile, said fee assessments are automatically generated based on the schedules under the ordinance and advised business owners with billing concerns to coordinate with the appropriate city departments.
Supreme Court junks plea
The implementation of the garbage fee ordinance was challenged before the Supreme Court on February 5, 2026.

The petition was filed by Las Piñas-based senior high school teacher John Barry Tayam, who invoked the "doctrine of transcendental importance" and sought a temporary restraining order against the implementation of the ordinance.
In a February 25 resolution, however, the Supreme Court dismissed the petition, ruling that Tayam lacked legal standing for not being a Manila resident.
It also ruled that the petitioner violated the doctrine of hierarchy of courts by filing the case directly with the high tribunal. — with additional reporting by Ella Mae Soriano

articles.title: What will Trump's retaliatory tariffs do to Canada’s economy big picture? Not that much, economists predict
articles.summary: With some tariffs added and others removed, economists predict that big picture the changes will break even. But certain industries will still be hit hard, they say, and the tit-for-tat will weigh on…

image.caption: Economists say this week's retaliation in the trade war will hurt some sectors and dent business confidence, but the sheer impact on the economy will be negligible. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

With some tariffs added and others removed, economists predict that big picture the changes will break even. But certain industries will still be hit hard, they say, and the tit-for-tat will weigh on business owners' confidence.
Real hit will be indirect, economists warn — as some businesses likely to feel relief, others 'horrified'
The White House fired another shot in the Canada-U.S. trade war this week, banning outright the imports of Canadian dairy, motorcycles and some alcohol products.
But how much will those bans, along with fresh 50 per cent tariffs on a slate of other products, actually impact the Canadian economy?
Not all that much, say economists who’ve run the numbers. But that doesn't mean it won't hurt certain industries — and it certainly won't give business owners any peace of mind.

On Tuesday night, the White House retaliated against Canada's counter-tariffs with the bans and the addition of 50 per cent tariffs to items including mattresses and some paper products. American officials also dropped tariffs on others, such as toilet paper, cement and sugar.

But according to one analysis from Derek Holt, vice president and head of capital markets economics at Scotiabank, the new tariffs will apply to an estimated $3 billion worth of Canadian goods, while the removed tariffs apply to about $2 billion worth — making the difference marginal, given Canada exported more than $527 billion worth of goods to the U.S. in 2025.

items: Trump banning import of Canadian booze, motorcycles, other goods into U.S.

blocks.text: The bans on alcohol, dairy and motorcycles will also be negligible, Holt adds, as Canada sends very little dairy and few motorcycles south of the border. Alcohol exports are a bit higher than the other categories, with $550 million worth sent to the U.S. last year, according to his analysis, but the export bans would still only impact $700 million worth of Canadian exports to the U.S.
"These actions are face saving by the U.S. administration, not substantive in nature and that’s a positive," Holt said in a note to investors on Wednesday.
How will the new U.S. retaliatory tariffs impact Canadians?

He says the rising cost of oil — which soared past $100 for the first time since July on Wednesday due to escalating tensions in the Middle East — poses a greater economic risk than the new U.S. measures.

At BMO, chief economist Doug Porter agrees. His team puts the value of newly tariffed items and those taken off the list both at about $2 billion, putting the country "in the same spot" as it was before the announcement.
But where the tariffs do hit, in certain industries or parts of the country, they will still hurt business owners badly, Porter told CBC News.

items: Just Asking wants to know: What questions do you have about shopping in the age of the Canada-U.S. trade dispute? Send us your questions before our Sept. 12 show.

blocks.text: "It's extremely negative for the new industries and products that were selected, but of course, some pretty important ones were taken off the list," he said.
"So there are going to be some relieved industries today and some horrified."
50% tariffs already an effective ban

For makers of Canadian booze, further escalation isn't a positive sign. Cal Bricker, CEO of Spirits Canada, says Canada exports much of the alcohol it makes to the U.S., making the continued targeting of his industry a concern.
U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol would bite deep, Spirits Canada says
But because many alcohol products already faced 50 per cent tariffs, upping the ante to a ban might not make a material difference to many booze producers.
Matt Johnston of craft brewer Collective Arts in Hamilton, Ont., says he wouldn't have been able to send any more of his beer south at a 50 per cent rate anyway.
"The reality is that once you add 50 per cent tariffs, it becomes extremely difficult to try and sell on the market.”

He already sent months worth of product to the U.S. before the new tariffs came into effect a few weeks ago, in hopes a deal could be reached before supplies ran out. Now, the plan is to grow the business within Canada and other international markets to make up for the loss of U.S. sales, where a fifth of their business used to come from.
"The world's a big place and we can look elsewhere," Johnston said.

As with alcohol, many of the banned items were already facing 50 per cent tariffs, RBC economist Nathan Janzen points out, which would have effectively kept them out of the U.S. market, meaning the impact of the ban will be relatively small.
Real hit will be indirect
Even if the impact will be small by the numbers, Tu Nguyen, an economist at accounting firm RSM Canada, says the escalation is still very real in terms of the message it sends to business owners.

While the U.S. has historically increased the tariff percentages in order to turn up the heat on Canada, Nguyen says an all-out ban signals a departure from that strategy. She says the real hit from the escalating retaliation will be indirect — the tit for tat denting business confidence.
"A lot of these tariffs, they sound really big … but they don't hit the economy nearly as badly as one would think," Nguyen said.
“The bigger hit, I would say … comes from uncertainty.”

And unlike in the past, when the U.S. gave many weeks or months of lead time before tariffs went into effect, some of the newly announced measures will come into force as soon as next week. Nguyen says this gives businesses less time to prepare or pivot to new markets, and introduces another worry for business owners on both sides of the border.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.

articles.title: American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?
articles.summary: The LA Rams will face the San Francisco 49ers in the first regular season American football game to be played Down Under.

blocks.text: American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?

blocks.caption: Image caption, George Kittle of the San Francisco 49ers and other players were greeted by fans in Melbourne this week

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied: San Francisco 49ers
George Kittle of the San Francisco 49ers and other players were greeted by fans in Melbourne this week
BySimon Atkinson
Australia producer
An oval ball, in September, in Melbourne usually means just one thing - the business end of the Australian rules football (AFL) season.
But on Friday, at the unsportingly early time of 7am, 100,000 people will begin filing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) for a very un-Australian sporting spectacle - American football.
The LA Rams take on the San Francisco 49ers in their opening National Football League (NFL) fixture, the first time the country has hosted a meaningful, non-exhibition regular season game.

The match sold out months ago, with more than half the crowd expected to be people living outside the state of Victoria. On the official ticket resale site, a restricted view seat is priced at more than A$650 (£350/US$470).
"Walking down the street, it's AFL finals week and you wouldn't even know," says Thomas McMillan, host of the NFL podcast Any Given Sunday Australia.

"It's all NFL everywhere. There are bars that are nothing but 49ers bars or Rams bars. We have a Ram Tram getting around the district. When you're in Melbourne and AFL isn't visible, it shows how big this is at the moment."
Kickoff at 10.35am local time on Friday may not be typical for local fans, but meets the demands of prime time US television schedules and their advertisers.
The league held its first international match in 2007, and over the past two decades the overseas matches have become a long-term strategy to attract supporters and their dollars.
Nine games outside the US are scheduled for the upcoming season, including three in London. But Melbourne is the furthest that players and US-based fans will have to travel.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fans admire an LA Rams mural in a Melbourne laneway

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied: LA Rams
Fans admire an LA Rams mural in a Melbourne laneway
"Obviously there are question marks when you hear you are playing in Australia," 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey told a press conference this week.
"But it has been so cool… the food's incredible, the coffee's great."
That caffeine reference was perhaps as much to the time zone, as nod to the city's famous café culture.

Melbourne is a mind-warping 17 hours ahead of California where both teams are based, and much of the pre-match attention has been on the two teams and their contrasting approaches to trying to "beat" the jet lag.
For the 49ers, who arrived late last week, their players have had time to get over the long journey, adjust to the time zone, acclimatise and practice at a nearby stadium.

Controversially, the LA Rams are taking things to the other extreme, planning to arrive on Thursday morning local time on a charted Qantas A380 superjumbo, play on Friday, and get back to the US west coast shortly afterwards, in theory to prepare for their next match with minimum disruption to the player's body clocks.
"Definitely it's a gamble," says McMillan. "If they don't quite get things right after the 16-hour flight, you still might have that jet lag, even though you're trying to avoid it."
"And not everyone can sleep on planes," says his co-host Danny Webb. "Whether you're in first class, business class, whatever it is, you're still on a plane."
"And", adds McMillan: "And they're six foot six most of them, so it's going to be even tighter seats".

Despite it technically being a "home" game for the Rams, who bid for NFL marketing rights in Australia under the leagues Global Markets programme, this all means it is the San Francisco 49ers that have more of a presence around Melbourne this week.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Former NFL players Joe Nedney (left) and Jesse Sapolu attend a "sausage sizzle"

blocks.text: Former NFL players Joe Nedney (left) and Jesse Sapolu attend a "sausage sizzle"

And while most practice sessions have been behind closed doors, there have been player appearances at a rally for fans and an AFL match, while ex-stars turned up at that most Australian of traditions, the weekly fundraising "sausage sizzle" at the country's most high-profile hardware chain.

American sports journalist Dontay Atkinson predicts this fan engagement will be reflected inside the stadium and that the MCG will be "heavily red" (the 49ers colour), accusing the Rams of doing "exactly jack squat to sell the NFL brand or connect with Australians".
Writing on X he added: "Fly in, fly out, no contact. I'm sure the Aussies feel great about that snub."
McMillan says he can understand the approach by the Rams, who are seen as contenders for the 2027 Superbowl.
"They're looking at this as a game they need to win," he says.
"We do feel a bit snubbed, and feel the 49ers are doing the right thing,
"But it is their job, so that's where the Rams coaching staff has gone 'nah, we're taking this approach'.
"I just worry that they have missed the boat of ingraining themselves as the Australian team. It leaves it open for others, and the 49ers have really jumped on that."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cheerleaders for the San Francisco 49ers dance in Melbourne's Federation Square

blocks.text: Cheerleaders for the San Francisco 49ers dance in Melbourne's Federation Square

The LA Rams insist there has been no snub, though speaking to the BBC, the club's Head of International Stephanie Cheng dodged the question of whether she would have preferred her players to have been in town this week.
"It's really a culmination of more than four years of work," she said. "It's not just about game week. We have long term rights."

Cheng says the Rams are the only NFL team with a membership programme for Australian fans, and that it has sent coaches into schools and communities to promote "flag football" – the non-contact version of the sport which will feature in the LA 2028 Olympics.

She also points to regular earlier visits by star players including running back Kyren Williams in March. This week its cheerleaders have visited US military bases in Australia before coming to Melbourne, and the franchise has installed a 22-yard floating football field on Melbourne's Yarra River serving as a fan zone.
"From day one, when we've come to Australia, there's been incredible enthusiasm," Cheng said.
While no Australian players will be on the field on Friday, there are dozens playing US college football and a handful in the NFL.
Most are punters, kicking specialists tapped up after showing their prowess playing AFL or rugby league.

But it is the success of Jordan Mailata, an offensive left tackle with the Philadelphia Eagles, who in 2025 became the first Australian to play in, and win, a Superbowl that was a "major turning point in Australia's fandom of the NFL " says Webb.
"Seeing an Australian in what we'd called a skilled position and then winning a Superbowl. It doesn't get better than that".
Friday's game is the first of three matches in Melbourne to be held over four years, under a contract between the NFL and the state of Victoria.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The LA Rams hosted a community day for American football fans in the run-up to the Melbourne match

blocks.text: The LA Rams hosted a community day for American football fans in the run-up to the Melbourne match
The league's preference, says Gerrit Meier, managing director and head of NFL International, is to have annual games in Australia similar, to the way the game has grown in the UK.
"We're working off the hypothesis that we need to make a commitment to a market," he told Reuters.

And while many US-based supporters are not fans of the international fixtures, these games are here to stay, says Webb, and the hype and the sell-out crowd in Australia augurs well for it to become a long-term fixture,
"I had mates four years ago asking why are you doing an NFL podcast? It's not a big sport here," he said.
"And now every single one of those mates are asking me for tickets for the game."

articles.title: Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment
articles.summary: Google has announced a plan to expand AI data centers and buy massive amounts of nuclear energy. Finland's security services have warned of there are risks, but the right-wing government says the…

image.caption: Google has signed a deal to purchase half of the energy produced at the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant over the next 22 yearsImage: Anne Kauranen/REUTERS

blocks.text: US tech company Google on Wednesday announced that it would be investing €13 billion ($15.1 billion) in AI infrastructure in Finland as well as penning a massive deal to buy nuclear power in the Nordic country over the next two decades.

This year, Google parent company Alphabet increased global investment to around $200 billion as it rushes to catch up in the AI race. Wednesday's announced deal is Google's biggest single investment in the EU to date.
Since repurposing a former paper mill in the coastal city of Hamina in 2009 and transforming it into a data center, Google has steadily increased its presence in the country.

The northern location offers two advantages, cold Arctic temperatures mean it needs less energy to cool energy hungry servers and the fact that Finland only has 6 million residents would seem to provide relief from the growing resistance that such projects are running up against in the US and elsewhere.

Google is not alone in looking to chilly Finland with its cheap nuclear, wind and hydroelectric energy supply to expand its business — Microsoft and TikTok parent ByteDance have also set up shop — with dozens of data centers being built in the country over the past few years.
Attracting data center investment has been a priority for Finland's right-wing Prime Minister Petteri Orpo as the nation confronts record unemployment and slow economic growth.
Why communities are fighting AI data centers
Google makes big claims about boosting Finnish GDP and creating jobs

In a statement, Google said the investment, scheduled to be doled out in 2027 and 2028, will include data centers, electrical grid improvement, and clean energy and battery projects for its chatbot, search and map services.
The company claims the investment will pump some €3.6 billion into Finland's GDP and create 37,000 jobs, with 7,000 being permanent and others coming during the construction phase.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo echoed Google's rosy outlook for his country's economy, emphasizing that it would spur further investment while downplaying fears that Google's project could drive up energy prices and gobble up resources."This investment is historical in Finland," said Orpo. "This makes us a front-runner in digitalization and AI."
Orpo said Google is, "committed to ensuring that electricity production in Finland ⁠remains sufficient and that prices remain under ​control."
The tax-avoiding US company said the deal was, "a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure."

"Now we are building more in Hamina, expanding that site on a remarkable level, and we are opening up data center operations in three new locations in the municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala," said Antti Jarvinen, the company's director of operations for Finland.
Resources under pressure
Beyond skyrocketing energy consumption, Finland's data center boom presents a potential security risk

Wednesday's deal also includes a purchase agreement for 50% of energy output from one of Finland's two nuclear power plants for the next 22 years according to plant operator Fortum, which will team up with the tech giant to explore new nuclear and renewable projects in the country.
Fortum shares jumped 15.5% on news of the deal, pushing them to their highest level in over four years and making the company the biggest winner on European stock exchanges for the day.
"We call this BYOP — bring your own power," ‌said Google President and ​Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat, who noted, "This is Google's first nuclear energy deal outside of the United States."

Fortum said the deal would allow it to "continue operating the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant until the end of its operating licenses in 2050," adding that without it, the plant, which currently supplies about 10% of Finland's electricity, would not have been able to continue operations past 2030.
Overall, Finland's data center boom is expected to create a massive spike in energy consumption, with network operator Fingrid forecasting a 40% jump over the coming years.

Beyond the environmental and energy concerns raised by such deals, Finland's Security and Intelligence Service (SUPO) has also issued explicit warnings that foreign-owned data centers pose potential security risks for the Nordic nation.

SUPO is concerned that municipalities may be weighing the economic potential of data centers more heavily than the security risk associated with them, noting that despite data center investments being fundamentally good for Finland there may be concerns if their owners are linked to authoritarian countries like Russia or China.

SUPO says authoritarian states may, for instance, try to use Finland to circumvent restrictions and sanctions on technology exports. For example, for advanced chips currently banned from export to China.
AI under pressure: scams, security and sustainability

articles.title: Notorious Ecuadorian crime gang designated a terrorist group by US
articles.summary:
Trump administration to seek extra funding from Congress to ‘dismantle’ Los Tiguerones over narcotics trafficking

The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which

blocks.text: The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which stormed a television station during a live broadcast in 2024, as a terrorist organisation as the Trump administration expands its campaign against narcotics traffickers it says are destabilising Latin America.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, made the announcement in Quito, where he met Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, one of several rightwing allies of Donald Trump whom Rubio is courting as a security partner during a three-nation tour through Latin America that began on Tuesday.
Rubio said the Los Tiguerones gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists.

“We are not talking about an ordinary mafia, nor are we talking about common criminals, we are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said.

The heavily armed gang’s attack on the TC Televisión network in 2024 prompted Noboa to declare a state of “internal armed conflict”, amid claims foreign drug gangs had descended on Ecuador to take control of important routes for coca grown in neighbouring Colombia and Peru and then shipped to the US.

Live footage from the El Noticiero news programme showed men toting pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and sticks of dynamite. The viral images quickly became a symbol of the drug violence destabilising the country.

In its efforts to fight against narcotics trafficking and illegal migration from Latin America, the Trump administration has also empowered a number of hardline leaders through its “Shield of the Americas” coalition that aims to tighten security cooperation with rightwing allies in the region.
During his trip, Rubio plans to visit several newly elected conservative leaders amid a significant political shift to the right in Latin America.

On Wednesday, Rubio hailed Ecuador as being the Trump administration’s most “aggressive” partner in its military campaign against alleged drug traffickers, including in the controversial strikes against boats that have killed at least 227 people whom the Trump administration has called drug traffickers without providing evidence.

Rubio said that he would seek $45m (£33m) in additional funding from Congress towards efforts aimed at “dismantling these terrorist groups”, although he did not go into details. He also told reporters that elite forces from both countries were “working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organisations”.

blocks.caption: Marco Rubio (left) is welcomed to Ecuador on Wednesday by its president, Daniel Noboa  Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Rubio visited Colombia on Tuesday, where he met its newly inaugurated president Abelardo De La Espriella, who narrowly won a June election against leftist leader Gustavo Petro with whom the Trump White House had cold relations.

During his remarks, Rubio took something of a victory lap, saying that the two sides would seek to “[confront] the mistakes of the past four years” and called Petro’s leadership of the country “unnatural”. Colombia joined the Shield of the Americas initiative only after its change in government.
During the meeting, the two men discussed security and counternarcotics policy, and signed memorandums of understanding on critical minerals and nuclear energy.

Rubio is expected to next travel to Peru, where he will meet Keiko Fujimori, who defeated a leftwing candidate by a margin of just 50,000 votes during a close election in July. She has promised to fight crime with an “iron fist” and adopt some controversial policies from neighbouring El Salvador, which has been a close ally of the US on security policies.

articles.title: Land in limbo: BBC visits West Bank village in area earmarked by Israel for settlement
articles.summary: BBC's Middle East Correspondent Lucy Williamson visits the Palestinian community of Khan al Ahmar in the so-called E1 area, and the neighbouring Israeli settlement of Maale Admumim.

blocks.text: UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank have triggered a series of Israeli counter-measures against UK nationals and organisations.

The sanctions came after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of settlement homes in the strategically important so-called E1 area east of Jerusalem, plans that have drawn widespread international condemnation.
The development would in effect divide the West Bank in two, and isolate East Jerusalem.
The BBC's Middle East Correspondent Lucy Williamson has been to the Palestinian community of Khan al Ahmar in the E1 area, and also to the neighbouring Israeli settlement of Maale Admumim.

articles.title: Buffalo Bills to 'celebrate' O Canada at home opener amid more Trump threats during trade war
articles.summary: Amid a trade war that includes President Donald Trump's threats to Canadian sovereignty and his vow to ban imports of several Canadian products to the U.S., the NFL's Buffalo Bills have made an…

image.caption: The NFL's Buffalo Bills say the Canadian national anthem will be played alongside the U.S. national anthem at the team's home opener on Sept. 13 against the Detroit Lions. (Adrian Kraus/Associated Press)

blocks.text: Hamilton

Amid a trade war that includes President Donald Trump's threats to Canadian sovereignty and his vow to ban imports of several Canadian products to the U.S., the NFL's Buffalo Bills have made an unexpected announcement.
NFL team says O Canada and The Star-Spangled Banner will be performed Sept. 17

Amid a trade war that includes President Donald Trump's threats to Canadian sovereignty and his plan to ban imports of several Canadian products to the U.S., the NFL's Buffalo Bills have made an unexpected announcement.

On Wednesday, the team said on social media platform X that both O Canada and The Star-Spangled Banner will be performed before its Sept. 17 home opener against the Detroit Lions, the first regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium.

The Bills announced that "for the first time in Highmark Stadium history, we will celebrate the American and Canadian anthems during pregame." Actress and singer Auliʻi Cravalho will perform the American anthem and Toronto band Barenaked Ladies will sing O Canada.

items: 'Unhinged' for Canada to call dispute with U.S. a trade war, says Trump's tariff chief

blocks.text: In Buffalo, the Canadian national anthem is rarely heard before NFL games, but it's commonly played before NHL games, even when the Sabres are up against American opponents. In April, fans at KeyBank Center in Buffalo sang O Canada after a microphone failed before the Sabres' playoff game against the Boston Bruins.

items: #TheMoment Buffalo Sabres fans sang O Canada after a mic failed

blocks.text: Buffalo is the only U.S.-based NHL team that plays both national anthems before home games against American and Canadian teams.
Tit-for-tat tariffs escalate trade war

On Tuesday, Trump signed five proclamations to ban Canadian imports including alcohol, motorcycles and various other products to the U.S. as of Sept. 29, and slap 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products starting next week.
The latest move in an escalating trade war between Canada and the U.S. comes after Canadian retaliatory tariffs, promised after trade talks fell apart last month, came into force Tuesday.

In explaining why Canada chose not to sign a trade deal amid Trump's deep tariffs on billions in Canadian goods, Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries."
Bills owners Terry and Kim Pegula bought the team for $1.4 billion US from the estate of late Hall of Fame owner Ralph Wilson in 2014.

items: Vince Carter, Tracy McGrady among 10 limited partners joining Bills' ownership group

blocks.text: NBA Hall of Famers Vince Carter and Tracy McGrady, former Toronto Raptors stars, were among 10 limited partners who joined the Bills' ownership group in 2024. Jozy Altidore, a former U.S. National Team soccer player, MLS champion and Toronto FC star, was also among the new limited partners announced.
It marked the first time in franchise history that minority owners were added.
