articles.title: Oil prices rise as Middle East conflict escalates
articles.summary: The price of oil returned to triple digits in US dollars, as conflict in the Middle East threatens supply chains and puts a strain on global reserves.

image.caption: Brent crude rose above $100 a barrel for the first time since JulyImage: Maxim Shemetov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Oil crude prices topped $100 ($86) a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July amid concerns over oil supplies due to the conflict in the Middle East.

"The move towards and back above $100 Brent is reflecting a market that increasingly must change its view on how long the Middle East crisis will continue to curb supply from the region," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at the Danish Saxo Bank.
The attacks on Saudi energy facilities by the Iranian-backed Houthisthreaten oil shipments on the Red Sea. This has been a key alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz path.

Meanwhile, the US attacked Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and in the Strait of Hormuz. "Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies," CENTCOM said in a statement.
Runing out of stock
Since the conflict in the Middle East started, oil exports have been reduced significantly, making some countries turn to their reserves.

The US has reported its lowest oil reserve since 1982, holding 289.7 million barrels. Former US President Joe Biden and President Donald Trump have used the reserve to cushion consumer prices amid the crisis.

The new price of the barrel is still below the peak reached early this year. In April, Brent jumped to $126 a barrel. Experts believe this is a big risk to a market with little room for capacity to absorb new disruptions occasioned by the war.

articles.title: Syria arms depot explosion kills at least 14
articles.summary: The explosion struck near the Syrian city of Sarmada in Idlib province in the northwest. The Defense Ministry said the weapons and remnants from the war were being stored temporarily at the site…

image.caption: The large explosion led to secondary explosions and fires that it took several hours to controlImage: Moawia Atrash/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Syrian authorities reported that at least 14 people were killed and another 11 wounded on Wednesday as a result of an explosion at a temporary site used to store weapons and remnants of the country's long-running civil war.
The explosion took place near the city of Sarmada in the northwestern Idlib province.

blocks.caption: Emergency services and Red Cross workers rushed to locate and if possible rescue victims potentially trapped beneath the rubble Image: Moawia Atrash/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What do we know about the explosion?
Syria's Defense Ministry said the weapons and war remnants were being stored termporarily at the site before being transported elsewhere. It said that some of its personnel were among those wounded.
The explosion in an area full of volatile materials led to secondary explosions and fires that hampered the emergency response. Smoke billowed from the blast site for some time on Wednesday.

"The toll from the explosion in a temporary storage for collecting weapons and war remnants near the city of Sarmada ... registered 14 killed and 11 injured in a preliminary count," the Idlib health department said.

blocks.caption: Firefigthers battled to bring the primary and secondary fires under controlImage: Kasim Yusuf/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Authorities have not yet said what caused the explosion.
It was the second fatal incident of its kind in Idlib province this month. On September 1, five people were killed and others were wounded when a vehicle carrying ammunition exploded in Binnish.

Syria only recently emerged from more than a decade of civil war, when forces loyal to new President Ahmed al-Sharaa ousted Bashar Assad and took control of Damascus. Idlib was one of the hardest-hit regions in the country during the war.

blocks.caption: Idlib province is still awash with ordnance after fierce fighting from 2011 until late 2024Image: Kasim Yusuf/Anadolu/picture alliance

articles.title: How Belarusians still find hope in a silenced country
articles.summary: The documentary "Letters From the Silenced Country" depicts the ongoing repression under the authoritarian regime. Director Andrei Kutsila talked to DW ahead of the film's Venice premiere.

image.caption: The film 'Letters From the Silenced Country' also features animated sequencesImage: DW/ZDF/Arte

blocks.text: When Belarusians took to the streets in 2020 to protest against the disputed results of the presidential election, hopes were high that the regime of autocratic ruler Alexander Lukashenko would end, and that Belarusian society would find freedom.
But authorities responded with an unprecedented campaign of repression that continues to this day. All forms of dissent have essentially been silenced.
It's in this context that filmmaker Andrei Kutsila directed a new documentary that depicts the state's system of repression.
His film, "Letters from the Silenced Country," was co-produced by DW and premieres at the Venice Film Festival on September 9.
A silenced country
Like the 300,000 to 500,000 Belarusians who now live in exile, Kutsila realized that he had to leave his home country amid the state's crackdown on free speech.

While he was completing his previous film — the award-winning "When Flowers Are Not Silent" (2021), on the state's brutal suppression of demonstrations — different colleagues around him were arrested, he says.
Many of them have since been released, "but at the same time, new prisoners are found to keep filling the cells. The situation is not changing; it's even worse now," Kutsila tells DW.
As the film points out in a postscript card, the human rights organization Viasna has documented at least 65,000 politically motivated arrests and detentions in Belarus since the 2020 protests.

"From the outside, people live their normal lives, but the streets have become quiet and conversations are reduced to whispers," says Kutsila. Those who remained in the country can get arrested and sent to prison simply for posting Belarusian symbols of freedom and resistance online, notes the filmmaker.
That was one of the reasons that motivated him to make "Letters from the Silenced Country."
Returning to Belarus and to physically meet and film protagonists in his home country was not an option, so he searched for an alternative way to portray their situation after the protests.
Letters to prisoners served as a starting point to Kutsila's film project: "I read thousands of them," he says.
He then picked stories of individuals — political prisoners, exiles and underground activists — who embodied different aspects of the situation.

blocks.caption: Footage from Belarusian prisons exposes harsh conditions for political detaineesImage: DW/ZDF/Arte

blocks.text: Vitold Ashurak died in prison
Belarusian opposition activist and environmental campaigner Vitold Ashurak is one of the film's protagonists.
Sentenced to five years in prison for participating in the protests, Ashurak's fate is portrayed through his correspondence with friends and family during his imprisonment.
Letters from a friend include meticulously selected photographs. Ashurak finds brief moments of mental freedom in these pictures, while the same images are also poetically embedded in the film.

But CCTV footage showing prison guards beating inmates brings viewers back to the brutal reality: Vitold Ashurak died under suspicious circumstances while in custody. His name is remembered as a symbol of the state's repression.
Between resignation and hope
The film also includes animated sequences, based on drawings created by the young student Kasia Budzko, who was sentenced to 2 1/2 years in prison for participating in protests.

Another protagonist in the film is Andrei Ostapovich, a former criminal investigator. In August 2020, he left his position, writing a letter of resignation in which he denounced the police officers' brutality against protesters.

blocks.caption: In the film, Ostapovich describes the sadistic tendencies he saw among the police forceImage: DW/ZDF/Arte

blocks.text: As one of the first security officials who publicly and categorically opposed the Belarusian regime, Ostapovich fled the country — facing many perilous detours.

In one scene of "Letters from the Silenced Country," Ostapovich is asked if, after everything he's been through and witnessed, he still believes in a free Belarus. After much hesitation, his only response is a sigh of resignation.

Filmmaker Andrei Kutsila shares this ambivalence: "Of course, it's in a way my perspective too, as I tried to express my feelings through my protagonists." But, Kutsila focuses on long-term progress, as he adds, "history is the foundation on which we can build a free country."
"You know, 200 years ago Belarus didn't even exist on a map," he points out. There have been struggles to free the country ever since: "So from this long-term perspective, there is a lot of hope."

"No matter how awful the situation is, the only thing that can empower and give us hope is solidarity, connection between people and love. So these are the things giving us hope," notes Kutsila. "And the film, I think, shows this."

articles.title: Why we're still looking for dark matter
articles.summary: When physicists said they may have spotted evidence of dark matter almost 100 years after it was proposed as a theory, the internet lit up. Here's why we're searching for the thing that holds…

image.caption: Dark matter: the thing that glues everything else in the universe together Image: Peopleimages Com/peopleimages.com/IMAGO

blocks.text: On September 1, 2026, scientists at a dark matter detector called LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) reported they had observed an event, a particle interaction, that they were unable to explain.

The team, based in South Dakota in the US, said the event resembled what they think a dark matter particle should produce when it collides with liquid xenon, one of a range of materials used for detecting dark matter.
They stopped short of calling it the discovery, or proof of dark matter, that many in the field have been hunting for almost 100 years.
The term "dark matter" was coined by physicist Fritz Zwicky in 1933 as a means to describe unseen matter that would explain fast-moving galaxies.

The LUX-ZEPLIN observation came just days after the release of the second season of Dark Matter, a sci-fi thriller starring Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly. Both events pushed the term "dark matter" back into people's minds.
Here's what you need to know, with the science separated from the series.
What is dark matter in simple terms?
Dark matter is often described as an "invisible" substance. But it may be better described as "transparent" because it can be seen, or detected, by the gravitational attraction it exerts.
That said, it neither emits nor reflects light, and has never been observed directly. So, in that sense, it is invisible.
Is it true that 95% of the universe is invisible?
Yes, roughly.
Ordinary matter — everything that can be seen or touched — accounts for about 5% of the universe.
Dark matter accounts for about 27%, and dark energy, a separate force linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe, about 68%. Together they account for about 95%.
A different figure of 85% is dark matter's share of matter alone.
But does dark matter really exist?

The strongest evidence that dark matter exists comes from the so-called Bullet Cluster, which formed when two galaxy clusters collided. The collision produced hot gas clouds that interacted. This interaction showed revealed mass in the gas clouds that distributed differently from the gas. Researchers said that mass could be dark matter.
Earth spins at 1,670 km/h: Why don't we feel it?
How do scientists search for dark matter on Earth?
Scientists use detectors like the LUX-ZEPLIN that passively wait for interactions between naturally occurring particles and detect radiation.
They tend to be buried deep underground, where the surrounding rock blocks cosmic radiation that would otherwise distort signals.
They are built from materials chosen for their very low levels of trace radioactivity, so a genuine detection is not lost in background noise.

The LUX-ZEPLIN detector specifically works by watching for a faint flash of light and pulse of electric charge released when a passing particle strikes a liquid xenon particle. Liquid xenon, a noble gas, has good properties for detecting radiation.
What is dark matter made of?
The leading candidate particles are:
WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles, are the longest-standing theory. They are heavy and interact only rarely with ordinary matter.
Axions, which are lighter and behave more coherently than WIMPs. A team at Kyoto University, Japan, say data from Earth's magnetic field could be used to search for axions.
What does dark matter do to humans?

Dark matter passes through the body constantly, without measurable effect. Billions of candidate particles cross through a person every second, but only about ten strike a nucleus in the body over a year.
The resulting radiation exposure is far lower than what people receive from radon or cosmic rays.

articles.title: LIV Golf in financial turmoil: what's next for the sport?
articles.summary: Six months after Saudi Arabia pulled funding from the breakaway organization, LIV Golf have filed for bankruptcy protection. Several of the world's best players signed on to LIV, so where does that…

image.caption: Bryson DeChambeau is owed an estimated $5.7m by LIV GolfImage: Jerod Ringwald/IMAGN Images/REUTERS

blocks.text: What has happened to LIV golf?
The breakaway golf tour, launched with much fanfare, billions of dollars of investment and a string of the world's best players, in 2021. But on Tuesday it filed for bankruptcy protection in the US.

Bankruptcy protection is a way of keeping a company alive while it restructures its debts. In this case, LIV would be moving from being financed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), which pulled out in April, to being supported by BC Partners, a British investment firm.
"This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf," said the chief executive, Scott O'Neil.

According to documents related to the filing, LIV Golf has between $500m (€430 million) and $1bn in estimated liabilities to at least 1,000 creditors. This includes an estimated $45 million to a group of top players like Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m), Jon Rahm ($7.5m) and Dustin Johnson ($5.7m).

O'Neil added that LIV intends to move towards a "player-first ownership model" but detail is thin and there is currently no schedule in place for 2027. Most of LIV's staff were laid off earlier this year.
What has caused LIV golf to go bankrupt?

The sudden withdrawal of the PIF, which had invested an estimated $5 billion in LIV Golf, is the over-riding reason. At the time, the PIF said that LIV Golf was "no longer consistent with the current phase of PIF's investment strategy."

This was considered evidence of the project's failure to overthrow the established PGA Tour or make much in the way of money or impact. While the huge prize money on offer lured away several big names, many more remained with the PGA Tour.

While Tuesday's legal move may buy LIV time, the withdrawal of Saudi funding was so key to its business model that it gives O'Neil few options. To survive, it seems, they must keep at least some of their big-name players while slimming down dramatically.
Why is Saudi Arabia investing billions in sports?
Is this further evidence of Saudi Arabia pulling out of sport?

It certainly seems that investment in golf is a thing of the past for the oil-rich, Gulf state. There have also been withdrawals of funding for tournaments, clubs or organizations in snooker, women's tennis, rugby and football. Saudi Arabia also backed away from its commitment to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games.

Sport was a key part of Vision 2030, a pet project of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that aimed to diversify the Saudi economy and, in the eyes of many, also help launder its reputation through sport and other cultural assets.

blocks.caption: Saudi Arabia is scaling back many sporting plans, including for World Cup 2034Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

blocks.text: The uncertainty caused by conflict in the Middle East has meant even the vast wealth of the Saudi ruling class has taken a hit while projects like the resort of Trojena, set to be a key resort in those Winter Games, have been scaled back.

The same is true of Neom, a proposed World Cup venue for 2034. Planned as an entirely new type of city - 500-meter-high, built in a straight line and powered by renewable energy, Neom's construction has been significantly scaled back. The Guardian reported in late 2025 that several proposed World Cup stadium architects have been asked to rethink their plans to cut costs.
What will happen to the LIV golf players now?

That too is unclear. The PGA Tour and LIV Golf have always had a frosty relationship. Any player leaving to join LIV was immediately suspended from the PGA Tour, which runs all golf's major championships.

The 'returning member program', used by US golfer Brooks Koepka earlier this year to return to the PGA, briefly offered a potential pathway. It was designed as a "route back to elite performers who no longer have contractual limitations preventing them from complying with PGA Tour rules and regulations."

However it is was only open to players who left the PGA Tour at least two years ago and have won the The Players Championship or one of the four majors. DeChambeau, Cam Smith and Rahm were, therefore, the only players that qualified. But with that door now seemingly closed even to them, a return looks complex.

"I'm not part of the discussions but I'm pretty sure they aren't going to be welcomed back straight away," said Rory McIlroy, a six-time major winner who has been consistently critical of LIV, in August.

"They were offered this returning member program back in February, the one Brooks [Koepka] took, but that has come and gone and I think it was said at the time that the deal they get going forward if they decide to come back would not be as good at the one Brooks got. So I'd say it will be a tough road back."

articles.title: South Korean students help plant narra seedlings on Mt. Malarayat
articles.summary: LUCENA CITY — South Korean students joined a regreening activity that involved planting 100 narra tree seedlings at the foot of Mount Malarayat in Lipa City, Batangas, the Department of Environment…

blocks.text: LUCENA CITY — South Korean students joined a regreening activity that involved planting 100 narra tree seedlings at the foot of Mount Malarayat in Lipa City, Batangas, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) said.

In a report on Tuesday, Sept. 8, the DENR office in Calabarzon said its Lipa community environment and natural resources office (Cenro) had partnered with ASEZ (Save the Earth from A to Z), a university student volunteer group of the World Mission Society Church of God, for the activity in Barangay Malitlit.
The agency said the initiative aimed to support the continuing rehabilitation and maintenance of the country’s forests.

“The program highlighted the important role of the youth in addressing environmental concerns, as well as the fact that environmental protection is a global responsibility that knows no nationality,” the DENR said.
Cenro Lipa also emphasized the importance of engaging young people in environmental protection efforts.
“It is important to raise their awareness and encourage their active participation in initiatives aimed at protecting the environment and natural resources,” the DENR said.

The narra, which is the Philippines’ national tree, is a large leguminous tree that can grow 30 to 40 meters tall. It produces fragrant yellow flowers that attract bees and typically blooms from February to May.
The species faces increasing threats from illegal logging, habitat loss, land conversion, and unsustainable harvesting. /mcm

In a written statement, the City of Malibu said it ordered the evacuation of the houses in the street and set up a temporary shelter for evacuees.

articles.title: Conspiracy theories can provide answers, but not peace
articles.summary: Twenty-five years after 9/11, conspiracy theories about the terrorist attacks persist. But even as an attempt to make sense of a tragedy, psychologists say the benefit in conspiracy ideation or…

image.caption: Not even conspiracy theories help us come to terms with the unsettling events of September 11, 2001Image: Diane Bondareff/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Psychology is not an exact science. That may irk a few researchers in the field. But it is important to mention upfront: Researching the psychology of conspiracy theories — why people are drawn to believing them and the effect they have on those people — is a complicated field of research, and conclusions are difficult to derive.
That is due, in part, to one of the basic problems with psychology, whether it's in treatment or in research, and that is that it relies on people's self-awareness.

If we take the example of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, some people continue to maintain it was "inside job", orchestrated by a secretive and powerful club of evil doers in the US government, intent on controlling citizens' lives by fear. And that may be true. But it may also be true that you, as a believer in such a theory, have always felt powerful people — your parents or teachers — have controlled and curtailed your agency in life. You may even have a false memory of how the terrorist attacks evolved on that day in 2001. Then, if someone asked you, "What really happened?", could you really say it for sure? I couldn't.
Self-report data is an issue in conspiracy research
Whether as patients or participants in a study, we may be asked to "self-report" — to look inside ourselves and express how we feel and why.
Self-reporting is an established way of measuring conspiracies, said Neil Dagnall, a professor of psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University, in an interview with DW.
But self-report data are "not perfect," he added.

They can be difficult data to handle because each judgment a person makes about themselves is relative, inherently subjective, and open to outside influence and bias. People's answers can change from day-to-day, especially when they involve emotions or feelings about mental state, depending on a multitude of events and experiences in our lives. In addition, there is no common scale.

Say, for example, you and a friend were asked, "Are you happy?" You may both say "yes," but your reasons for doing so may be completely different and be subject to different variables. The same goes for a question like, "Do you believe in conspiracy theories?"

"The judgment I'm making is a relative one. What's my norm? Am I comparing it to my friends who don't believe in conspiracies or am I in a group of people who do believe in conspiracies? We're always making relative judgments about our psychological propensities," said Dagnall.
Which suggests we're unlikely to ever get a definitive answer. Self-report data suggest correlations, not causation.
In a study on conspiratorial beliefs and well-­being, which Dagnall co-authored and published in May 2026, "self-report data" was specifically highlighted as a limitation.

This makes it very difficult to assess whether "conspiracy belief" or "conspiracy ideation" is good or bad for people and their sense of well-being. Especially as people who seek and believe in conspiracy theories often start out with a skewed view of reality.
Brain health: How to protect mental fitness and memory
Observing behavior can offer clues
There are ways of "triangulating" self-­report data, as the authors of the study put it, to get a more reliable, objective reading of a person's emotional, or psychological, state.

For example, psychologists use behavioral observations, like measuring heart rate variability, or Galvanic Skin Responses such as the electrical conductance of a person's skin, which is affected by sweating under stress. You can also retest participants' self-reported data, and therefore its reliability, by asking the same questions at different points in time.

But there is another factor that complicates research into the psychology of conspiracy theories, and that is that they, and people who believe in them, are more common than we like to think or admit (even when we believe them ourselves).
"The idea that people who believe in conspiracies in general populations are remarkable or different is not true," said Dagnall.
The truth: 'conspiracies theories are common'

Most of us, at some point in our lives, are bound to see something strange or stressful in society and question whether we, as individuals or as a member of a group, accept the accepted truth of how that thing or event came about. It can be a healthy sign of a questioning mind.
There are positive examples of conspiracy theories that happened to kickstart investigations that then revealed the horrible truth of government corruption.
Take Partygate during the COVID pandemic in the UK or — the mother of all conspiracies — Watergate during the Nixon Administration in the US.
And there are other conspiracy theories, such as the one that nobody has ever landed on the moon, which you can either take seriously or laugh about.
It all comes down to "the degree to which we engage in conspiracies generally, and the extent to which they interfere and disrupt our everyday lives," said Dagnall.
For Dagnall, who doesn't believe in the 1969 moon landing, it doesn't seem to disrupt his daily life — at least, that is what he self-reported to DW.
Watergate Anniversary
But for some people, conspiracy theories are disruptive and can lead to a sustained sense of dissatisfaction.

"Ample studies suggest that exposure to conspiracy theories or belief in them might lead to more negative emotions, heightened anxiety, or even paranoid thoughts," said Zuzanna Molenda, a researcher at the Polish Academy of Sciences and lead-author of a 2023 study on emotion dysregulation and belief in conspiracy theories.

Some people may be primed to more readily believe in conspiracy theories because they generally struggle to deal with psychological threat and distress. When they then seek answers in conspiracy theories, their pre-existing negative psychology may be enhanced.

"If anything, the available evidence suggests that rather than help people manage difficult emotions, conspiracy beliefs may be accompanied by or contribute to further distress," wrote Molenda in an email to DW.
No long-term benefit from conspiracy belief
There may be some psychological benefit to conspiracy theories, said Molenda, but only in the short term.

"Conspiracy beliefs can provide people with a sense of explanation and understanding when events feel uncertain or difficult to make sense of. For some people, they might also be a source of entertainment and fun. For others, they can provide a sense of belonging and connection with others who share the same beliefs, and they can be an important part of social identity," Molenda said.
But these potential benefits do not necessarily translate into better well-being in the longer term, said Molenda.
In the end, we're all searching for meaning and purpose in life. If we find a satisfactory answer, it gives us, what psychologists call presense — a direction in life, and that is good.

But if your search only leads to more uncertainty, more anxiety, and more doubt in your purpose in life, then that's bad. "And people who believe in conspiracies are asking questions but not getting answers," said Dagnall.

articles.title: Policeman kills teacher wife at Thai school, kids safe: officials
articles.summary: BANGKOK, Thailand – A police officer shot dead his teacher wife at the kindergarten where she worked in Thailand on Wednesday but all the children are safe, officials said. The gunman returned…

blocks.text: BANGKOK, Thailand – A police officer shot dead his teacher wife at the kindergarten where she worked in Thailand on Wednesday but all the children are safe, officials said.
The gunman returned home after the shooting in Chonburi province, southeast of Bangkok, where police were negotiating his surrender.
The incident is the latest shooting to rock Thailand, a month after a teenager shot his grandparents and then five staff and a pupil at his school, before killing himself.
Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region, and past promises of tightening gun laws have not prevented repeated shootings.

Sayan Klomaon, chairman of Nong Pla Lai sub-district council, told AFP the gunman — a policeman local to the area — came to the school at about 10:30 am (0330 GMT) and talked with his wife before shooting her.
No students saw the incident, as it happened outside the classroom, he said, adding that the gunman then left to go home, and since then all the children had been picked up.
In a statement on Facebook, Chonburi Governor Naris Niramaiwong confirmed that all 44 children were safely evacuated along with three teachers and three other staff members.
He said police had surrounded the house where the gunman was and were negotiating his surrender.
The motive remains unclear.
Naris ordered the kindergarten closed and said psychological support will be provided to children and staff who witnessed the incident.
In 2022, an ex-policeman armed with a gun and a knife stormed a nursery in northern Thailand and killed 24 children and 12 adults, in one of the country’s deadliest massacres.

articles.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
articles.summary: Traffickers are making big bucks smuggling millions of critically endangered eels across continents, in suitcases on planes or by exploiting legal loopholes to end up on dinnerplates. Where are the…

image.caption: Unai Eizaguirre, an eel fisherman for 30 years, prepares gear with a colleague in the Basque CountryImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades.

The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species, which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in illegally caught eels.

"So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous."

Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed.
"I don't know if the eel has time to wait for these projects to show their effects," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI.

blocks.caption: Marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says only 12% of eels now survive the journey from the Sargasso SeaImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: Eel smuggling as lucrative as drugs

Part of what makes European eels so vulnerable is their remarkable life cycle, which was, until relatively recently, a source of mystery. Scientists now know adult eels migrate thousands of kilometers from European rivers to the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic, their only known spawning grounds. They breed and then die, leaving their larvae to drift to Europe. By the time they reach rivers, they've transformed into tiny, transparent "glass eels."

Today, only about 12% survive the journey from the Sargasso to the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways, Diaz told DW. The young glass eels conservationists are trying to protect are the most valuable in the illegal trade, fetching up to €9000 ($10,400) per kilogram.

"You can compare it with drug trafficking. Every year they seize tons of illegally caught eel in Europe," said Eizaguirre. "The big business lies in trafficking them to Asia," adding that the huge profits and comparatively small fines for smaller infractions by local fishers make the risk worth it. However, when criminal organizations are involved, penalties can be substantial with fines up to 6 times the value of illegally smuggled eel.

Demand in countries such as China, South Korea and Japan is driving prices. As is a biological peculiarity: so far, it's been exceedingly difficult to get eels to reproduce in captivity. This means fish farms — where the eels are raised before being sold to premium restaurants — need a steady stream of young from the wild. Sometimes, the same smuggled eels come back to Europe as fillets for the sushi market.

Conservationists had hoped pressure on the species would ease when the EU banned export of the species outside the bloc in 2010. Instead, organized crime groups have increasingly muscled in on the market, with the illegal trade now generating an estimated €3 billion in profits in peak years.

"Our estimated maximum was always 100 tons of glass eels smuggled annually. That's already around 300 million fish," said Florian Stein, head of policy and science at the German Angling Association. But information from his contacts in the illegal trade have led him to the conclusion that it was a "very conservative estimate."
International law enforcement agencies are also cracking down, with Europol's Operation Lake seizing 22 tons of glass eels and arresting 26 suspects between 2024 and 2025.
"There has been a lot of pressure from law enforcement throughout Europe," said Interpol's Sanchez Romero. "That's why the criminal groups always look for new routes."

blocks.caption: A small dam near Plentzia — obstacles like this can block eels on their migration routeImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: Eels smuggled in plain sight in regular suitcases along complex routes

Still, Stein, who did his doctoral dissertation on international eel smuggling and advises the German government, said trafficking has increased since 2020, and illegal trade routes have become more complex.
"Ten years ago, Madrid airport was still one of the biggest smuggling hotspots," he said. This was due to its proximity to fishing grounds in northern Spain and Portugal.

Increased checks by Spanish authorities on flights to East Asia forced traffickers to adapt. Experts now say a new route running through North Africa via Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal has become increasingly important.

Geography is one reason the route is attractive. The Strait of Gibraltar is 14 kilometers at its narrowest point and a busy maritime junction. "We know that many drugs are also transported through this strait," Moroccan investigative journalist Yassir Al-Makhtoum told DW.

European eels also inhabit rivers and estuaries in Morocco. Though the country has banned the export of glass eels smaller than 12 centimeters (4.7 inches), it is building a legal domestic eel trading industry. Experts fear that's acting as a cover for trafficked animals coming in from Europe.

From Morocco, smugglers then move eels along numerous routes to Asia. The means are not always sophisticated. Glass eels can be transported in ordinary suitcases on domestic flights. They're placed in bags filled with a little water and insulated to keep their temperature stable. They can survive for up to 48 hours in those conditions. Once in Asia, they go to the fish farms.

blocks.caption: In Plentzia, where eel fishing has long been part of daily life, fishermen say the regional ban risks hurting those who follow the rules while illegal traders continue to profitImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: A species running out of time

Eels are an important indicator species for the health of ocean and riverine ecosystems because their long migrations across multiple habitats make them vulnerable to problems that could also harm other species. They also serve as important prey for herons, otters and larger fish.
"But the impact of its disappearance is difficult to predict," said marine biologist Diaz.

Under EU regulations, member states must undertake measures to allow 40% of adult eels to return to the Sargasso Sea to spawn. Diaz also wants to ensure at least 40% of glass eels make it back from the Sargasso Sea.

But European eels are not the only eel species under threat. A proposal to protect all freshwater eel species from illegal and unsustainable trade was rejected at the 2025 CITES wildlife conference. For Stein such protection is key.

"The proposal should be on the table again at the next conference. I just don't know how else we can get a handle on this problem," said Stein, adding more lobbying and coalition building is needed to advocate for a ban.

“The eel for us is more than just a fish,” said Unai Eizaguirre. “It's been part of our identity for centuries.” For fishermen like him, better protection for the eel represents a chance at a sustainable future.
The research for this story was sponsored by: The Med Mosaic.
Burundi's vanishing lakes and the fight to bring them back

articles.title: Tulfo on China’s note to Teodoro: ‘They shouldn’t have done that’
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Erwin Tulfo has criticized the Chinese delegate who passed a note to Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. while he was speaking at the Seoul Defense Dialogue, saying that…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Erwin Tulfo has criticized the Chinese delegate who passed a note to Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. while he was speaking at the Seoul Defense Dialogue, saying that it was improper.

Tulfo on Wednesday was referring to the incident in which Teodoro was handed a note supposedly from a Chinese military attaché at the Chinese Embassy in Seoul while discussing the importance of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos) at the forum on Tuesday.
The note dismissed the South China Sea arbitration, calling the 2016 award “illegal, null, and void.”
“They shouldn’t have done that,” Tulfo told the media in an ambush interview.
According to Tulfo, Teodoro’s response to the note was commendable, saying that if he were in Teodoro’s position, he might have gotten into trouble.
“That’s the right thing to do,” Tulfo said. “If I were handed that note, there might have been a problem… They might say it’s not something a senator should do, but I will really stand up.”
Upon receiving the note at the forum, Teodoro read portions of the message aloud, reacting in between.
When the message disregarded the Unclos decision, Teodoro pointed out that even China had signed the international framework.
The note also reiterated that China does not recognize the 2016 ruling. To this, Teodoro said, “Of course, because you lost.”
Teodoro also denounced the act of passing him a note in the middle of the forum, saying it was disrespectful to the organizers and guests, adding that China needs “basic decency and behavior.”
He also called the note “actual coercion, bullying and aggression,” which is a reminder of “China’s weak position.”
The audience at the forum applauded Teodoro afterward. /mcm

articles.title: Family of British man found dead in Grenada ask local police to work with UK investigators
articles.summary:
Andrew Frederick’s body was found in property he was staying at in Grenada in January

The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in…

blocks.text: The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in Grenada to work with UK police to uncover the truth about his death.

Andrew Frederick’s body was found in the property he was staying at in Grenada on 4 January. An autopsy, performed in the same week by a privately hired pathologist, concluded that the 47-year-old’s death was a homicide.

In June, Grenada’s director of public prosecution, Howard Pinnock, said at a press conference that Frederick’s and another pending case would be sent to the coroner to determine the cause of death “because there is no basis in terms of both investigations that any homicide has occurred”.
After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK last month, where a second autopsy was carried out.
The UK coroner has noted that Frederick’s organs are missing and the death is currently “unascertained”.
At the start of an inquest at West London coroner’s court last week, senior coroner Lydia Brown said the Metropolitan police are now investigating Frederick’s death.

The family, who attended the court hearing by video link, said the coroner’s “decision to suspend Andrew’s inquest to allow the Metropolitan police to conduct a criminal investigation marks a significant turning point”.
In statement to the Guardian, they urged Grenada and the UK to work together to find out what happened to Frederick.

“We are encouraged and grateful that the Metropolitan police investigation is now under way. Justice for Andrew depends on everyone with the power to act, on both sides of the Atlantic, doing what is right,” the statement said.

It added: “Andrew was a deeply loved member of a close-knit family; a son, brother, father and grandson. He leaves behind his cherished daughter, who should be growing up with him beside her, not learning to live without him.

“Our family remain determined to uncover the truth about what happened to Andrew and to see justice follow. We hope this ruling is the step that finally enables a complete, properly coordinated investigation and that everyone who can assist will now do so.”

Earlier this year, the family had called for an urgent review of the policies governing UK assistance to the loved ones of Britons killed abroad, after they were forced to launch their own public appeals for information, and commission an independent forensic pathologist and a private investigation.

“Eight months have passed since Andrew was taken from us. In that time, we have learned what no family should ever have to learn, and fought battles no family should ever face alone,” their statement said.

It added: “We have relentlessly sought answers and support while carrying the weight of Andrew’s loss and the horror of what was done to him. We still do not have a complete account of what happened, and important questions remain unanswered.

“We hope the Grenadian authorities with knowledge of the case will now share that information and work collaboratively with the Metropolitan police, allowing the investigation to proceed without further delay. We are also seeking urgent answers as to why Andrew’s organs were absent when his body was returned to the UK for further examination.”
In Grenada, the Office of the Commissioner told the Guardian that “the matter will be progressing to the coroner’s court for the parish of Saint George”.
A Met spokesperson said: “The Met is investigating the death of 47-year-old Andrew Donald Frederick, who died in Grenada on 4 January.
“Mr Frederick’s family are being supported by specialist officers.
“No arrests have been made at this stage and inquiries are ongoing.”
Officers have contacted the Royal Grenada Police Force (RGPF) to offer assistance and discuss how the investigation can be progressed.
Inquest proceedings have been suspended pending the outcome of police investigations.

articles.title: ‘Too little response’ to Russian strikes on Ukraine, Zelenskyy says after latest deadly attacks – Europe live
articles.summary:
Ukrainian leader calls for more action from allies following overnight attacks in which two people died

At least two people died were injured in Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight,…

items: 18m agoMorning opening: 'Too little response' to Russian strikes on Ukraine, Zelenskyy says

blocks.text: Morning opening: 'Too little response' to Russian strikes on Ukraine, Zelenskyy says

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
At least two people died were injured in Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight, with Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying “there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes.”

blocks.caption: A firefighter inspects an apartment inside a residential building hit by a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

blocks.text: Two people were killed, three injured and 16 evacuated after a strike on the Starokozache border crossing with Moldova. Four people were injured after a Russian drone struck an apartment building in Kyiv. More strikes were reported in Dnipro, Mykolaiv, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia and Zhytomyr.

“A response is needed – Moscow must not go into the winter believing that it can get away with missile and drone terror without consequences. The aggression must be stopped here and now, before it spreads any further,” Zelenskyy said.
He called for “effective” sanctions against Russia and support for Ukraine, saying “the partners who can help know exactly what is needed every day.”

The Russian defence ministry said ⁠that its forces ⁠had struck a Ukrainian ⁠cargo vessel ​carrying ‌military equipment ‌in the ‌Black Sea en route to the port of ‌Odesa, as well as ​a warehouse in Kyiv, belonging ⁠to a company ​manufacturing drones, ​Russian ​news agencies ​reported.

Lots to cover.

Good morning.

articles.title: Nats boss summoned by UK transport secretary as flight chaos enters second day
articles.summary: Martin Rolfe, who faces pressure to resign, due to brief Heidi Alexander after cancellations hit 1,300

blocks.text: The boss of the air traffic control provider Nats has been summoned to meet the UK transport secretary as the number of flight cancellations hit 1,300 in a second day of disruption for hundreds of thousands of passengers.
Martin Rolfe, who is facing increasing pressure to resign over a third major stoppage to flights in just over three years, is due to brief Heidi Alexander on Wednesday.
Rolfe ruled out a cyber-attack as a cause for the “technical issue” at air traffic control and defended the resiliency of the systems run by Nats, which provides services to 15 UK airports.
“We will be doing a very thorough and full investigation,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “We have at this point ruled out a cyber-attack.

“I don’t believe we have ever seen an incident happen more than once. This will be something we haven’t seen in more than 50 years of operation. I would say the UK has one of the best reputations in the world both from a safety perspective and resilience perspective.”
Nats said the problem occurred in its flight processing system but was not the same fault as those that caused outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025.
However, Yvonne Moynihan, the managing director of Wizz Air UK, called on Rolfe to consider resigning over the repeated technical failures at Nats.
“In any industry when you’ve had three failures you need to consider three strikes and you’re out,” she told Today.

“A third time and a third excuse is not enough any more. What we need to see from leadership is accountability. There are serious questions about the resilience of the system. I think Nats and the leadership need to look deep inside themselves.”
On Tuesday, Nats said that the fix had been a “very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover”.
According to FlightRadar, 246 flights had been cancelled at Heathrow by 6am on Wednesday, while Gatwick passengers faced 33 cancellations.

In a statement on social media on Wednesday morning, Heathrow said: “Following yesterday’s Nats technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew.
“Please check your flight status with your airline before travelling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be operating.”
after newsletter promotion
In a statement on X, Gatwick also said flights had resumed but the disruption was likely to continue.

Ryanair has said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed and 50 flights cancelled, with the knock-on effects affecting flights across Europe. Europe’s biggest low-cost carrier repeated its demand for Rolfe to resign.

The airline’s chief operations officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Families travelling on holiday, people travelling for work and thousands of visitors to the UK have once again paid the price for Nats’ abhorrent failure.”
He said the government should “stop making excuses for repeated Nats failures and appoint a new leader capable of running the UK ATC system”.
The breakdown started at about 1pm on Tuesday and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted.
London airports, as well as Manchester and Birmingham, were among the most directly affected. Flights to and from other airports around the UK, including Edinburgh and Belfast, were also disrupted.

The air traffic control problems follow an “isolated event” a year ago that caused widespread disruption, and appeared less severe than the full grounding of flights in August 2023, which prompted a parliamentary inquiry.

articles.title: PNP: Indian, Korean men rescued from kidnap-for-ransom schemes
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — An Indian national and a Korean national were rescued by law enforcers in separate operations against kidnapping-for-ransom schemes, the Philippine National…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — An Indian national and a Korean national were rescued by law enforcers in separate operations against kidnapping-for-ransom schemes, the Philippine National Police–Anti-Kidnapping Group (PNP–AKG) said on Wednesday.

In a press briefing in Camp Crame, AKG director Brig. Gen. Edwin Balles detailed that last Saturday, operatives rescued a 24-year-old male Indian medical student along Alabang-Zapote Road in Las Piñas City.

The victim had been kidnapped from his apartment also in Las Piñas last Thursday night and was reported missing by his brother on Friday after receiving a message from the kidnappers demanding a P250,000 ransom, according to Balles.

He noted that the victim’s family had transferred 80,000 Indian rupees (roughly P52,500) to the suspects’ bank accounts and deposited P150,000 more at an automated teller machine along Alabang-Zapote Road upon the alleged kidnappers’ instructions.
The AKG director said operatives had monitored the suspects attempting to retrieve the deposited money but were then caught by police.
Balles only identified the arrested suspects as the victim’s schoolmates, five male individuals between ages 24 and 26.
“Parang sila yung siga-siga doon sa school nila na vini-victimize din nila yung mga kalahi nilang Indians,” Balles said of the suspects.
(They were like the gang in their school who victimized their fellow Indians.)

“Kinuha nila itong victim dahil gusto nilang gamitin yung crypto e-wallet account niya. However, nase-sense na nitong Indian victim na gagamitin nila in a criminal enterprise activity. Ayaw niya pumayag. With that, hineld captive na siya,” he added.

(They took this victim because they supposedly wanted to use their crypto electronic wallet account. However, the Indian victim sensed that they wanted to use the account for a criminal enterprise activity. He didn’t want them to do that. With that, they held him captive.)
“Dumudugo yung kanyang tenga,” Balles said of the victim. “Accordingly, kailangan operahan yung injury niya. Pinagsasampal siya.”
(His ear was bleeding. Accordingly, his injury needs to be operated. He had been slapped repeatedly.)
The arrested suspects were taken into police custody and underwent inquest proceedings for kidnapping and serious illegal detention.
Korean businessman rescued
Balles said AKG operatives also rescued a 41-year-old South Korean businessman in Pasay City early morning last Tuesday.
According to the AKG chief, the victim was plying Roxas Boulevard near Vicente Sotto Street when a silver sports utility vehicle stopped him and his companions by at least seven men.
The foreign national was forced to board the kidnappers’ car.
Balles said investigators so far believe that the individuals only targeted the foreigner for the ransom.

“After the kidnapping, nag-communicate kaagad sila sa isang known best friend niya na hawak na ng mga kidnapper yung kinuhang Koryano at may binanggit na nga silang initial demand na P30 million,” he explained.
(After the kidnapping, they had communicated with one of the victims’ known best friend that they had kidnapped the Korean and they mentioned an initial demand of P30 million.)
He noted that the victim’s family had electronically sent over roughly P550,000 worth of a mix of Philippine pesos and USDT, or the cryptocurrency Tether.
Balles said the foreigner was released shortly after the transaction in Kawit, Cavite before making his way back to Pasay City, where he was found.
He did not explain why the victim was released despite not meeting the ransom demanded nor how the victim managed to go from Kawit, Cavite to Pasay City.
“Nung nasa captive na siya, may narinig siyang nagpakilalang [pulis]. But, that is still subject to our conduct of case build-up,” Balles noted.
(When he was being held captive, he supposedly heard someone introducing themselves as a police officer. But, that is still subject to our conduct of case build-up.)
He added that the victim was arrested for alleged possession of illegal drugs last January but was released on bail.

The AKG chief also said investigators were now working to identify the seven individuals whom the victim supposedly saw; and looking to trace them through the financial accounts where the P550,000 ransom had been sent. /mr

articles.title: The Bayeux Tapestry in London: What's behind the hype?
articles.summary: The exhibition of the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum is eagerly anticipated across the UK, as the medieval masterpiece is considered by many to be a symbol of the country's identity.

image.caption: Masterpiece of the High Middle Ages: the Bayeux Tapestry (detail)Image: Bildagentur-online/picture alliance

blocks.text: First, let's start with a clarification: Strictly speaking, it's not actually a tapestry, since tapestries are woven, whereas this artwork is an embroidery on linen. Nevertheless, it is commonly referred to as such.

This pictorial narrative which is approximately 70 meters (230 feet) long, depicts the events surrounding the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, culminating in the Battle of Hastings and William the Conqueror's victory over Harold II.

The Norman Conquest radically changed England: politics, laws and culture all came under the influence of Norman rule. The Bayeux Tapestry bears witness to this event; at the same time, it is an outstanding example of English craftsmanship from the Middle Ages and is seen by many Britons as one of the most important symbols of British identity, alongside the works of Shakespeare or Stonehenge.

The tapestry is thought to have been commissioned by the Bishop of Bayeux, William's half-brother, who was present at the battle, from embroiderers in southern England for the opening of his cathedral in 1070. Anglo-Saxon embroiderers were famous throughout Europe at the time for their skills. The work then made its way to France, where it remained for almost a thousand years — until now.
Why is the Bayeux Tapestry so important?

The Bayeux Tapestry is considered one of the most important pictorial monuments of the High Middle Ages. Many researchers view it as an elaborately crafted piece of propaganda that showed and explained William the Conqueror's victory to people at the time. Its scientifically disputed message is that Harold Godwinson, then Earl of Wessex, had sworn a sacred oath on relics to support William's claim to the English throne. He broke this oath when he had himself crowned king. The war is therefore portrayed as his just punishment. The fact that Harold had probably not taken the oath of his own free will is irrelevant to this woven narrative.
The embroidery is part of the UNESCO Memory of the World Register and, because of its 58 pictorial scenes, is sometimes referred to as "the world's oldest comic."
Accompanied by Latin inscriptions, the pictorial narrative depicts the horrors of war — including massacres, rolling heads and the death of a king.

But it is also a valuable historical document for researchers. The tapestry illustrates shipbuilding and military equipment in surprising detail, as well as everyday medieval life. Even Halley's Comet is shown in it — the comet was visible in the sky in 1066 and was interpreted by the Anglo-Saxons as a bad omen in the pictorial narrative.

blocks.caption: Harold swearing the solemn oathImage: Pascal Deloche/Godong/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why did it take so long to get the tapestry on loan?
The tapestry is owned by the French state and had been placed on deposit with the City of Bayeux for display at the Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux.

Britain had already tried to borrow the tapestry for the coronation of Elizabeth II in 1953, as well as for various historical occasions afterwards, but France had always refused. The artefact was considered too fragile and the journey too risky. Finally, President Emmanuel Macron gave the green light last year for an exhibition at the British Museum — overriding the concerns of his experts.
Last September, the tapestry was taken down, packaged and initially placed in storage in a highly elaborate, six-hour procedure.

On July 9, it finally arrived in London in a secret transport operation, enclosed in a high-tech container that shielded it from all vibrations while maintaining a constant temperature and humidity level.
The British government has also insured the artwork for £800 million (around €932 million or $1 billion).

blocks.caption: Removing the 11th-century Bayeux Tapestry from its display in France took a meticulously coordinated team effort lasting several hoursImage: Lou Benoist/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Where can you get tickets?

The British Museum has divided ticket sales into three phases. The first, covering September to December, began on July 1. All tickets sold out quickly, with up to 80,000 people reportedly trying to secure a slot at the same time. Many had to wait up to nine hours.
For those who missed out, there will soon be another chance — tickets for January to March will go on sale on October 21, and tickets for April to July in January.
The exhibition is being marketed as a "once-in-a-generation" event, and an extensive educational program is intended to involve schools across the country.

The British Museum is optimistic that the Bayeux Tapestry will help it set a new visitor record. The most popular exhibition in the museum's history to date is the 1972 "The Treasures of Tutankhamun," which attracted almost 1.7 million visitors.
No ticket? Here's an alternative

If you're now eager to see the tapestry but unsure if you'll land a ticket, you can also head to the town of Reading, around two hours west of London. There, you can see a faithful replica of the tapestry, which is itself already 140 years old.

Even back then, there was a strong desire in England to have this artwork in the country. In 1885, 35 embroiderers set to work for around a year. Using colored photographs as a reference, they reproduced the tapestry on a one-to-one scale. However, they did change one detail: Some figures on the original border are naked and in suggestive poses. Apparently, this was considered too scandalous in Victorian England. One figure was retouched in the corresponding photograph — and the embroiderers copied the alteration. As a result, the figure is depicted wearing underwear.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: EU sports commissioner says FIFA is 'damaging to football'
articles.summary: Speaking to DW, EU Commissioner Glenn Micallef hit out at world football's governing body over its "poor governance".

image.caption: Glenn Micallef believes FIFA is damaging footballImage: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: The European Union's sports commissioner has criticized world football's governing body FIFA over its controversial and now-aborted plans to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Speaking to DW at his Brussels office, Commissioner Glenn Micallef labeled the plans "another episode in a series of poor governance decisions that excessively commercialize the sport," adding: "It's damaging to football."

However, Micallef stopped short of calling on FIFA President Gianni Infantino to resign, amid growing pressure on him to step down. Asked whether FIFA was fit for purpose under Infantino, the commissioner insisted it wasn't for him to decide.

"That's a decision that belongs to national associations and federations," Micallef said. "I hope that they will have the chance to have an open process where they can discuss these things, where they can ensure accountability and responsibility for these issues."
Infantino faces ethics complaint

Micallef's comments come as the human rights group FairSquare submitted an updated complaint against Infantino to FIFA's ethics committee, joined by more than 100,000 signatures as part of its "Reboot FIFA" campaign.

The complaint details eight instances, four of them new, in which Infantino allegedly broke FIFA's ethics rules. These include the World Cup privatization plans and the reversal of US player Folarin Balogun's red card ban. All of the instances are linked to Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump.

In the complaint seen by DW, FairSquare state: "at a minimum, [Infantino] abused his power, violated his duty of political neutrality and his duty of loyalty in his efforts to ingratiate himself with the US president. The evidence that he sought to gain personally from this pattern of behaviour adds to the seriousness of the allegations."
Nicholas McGeehan, director of FairSquare, told DW that European football's governing body UEFA — among Infantino's fiercest critics — should get behind the complaint.

"I think [the ethics committee] is a paper tiger, but it is a mechanism that could be usefully deployed," McGeehan said. "You have a mechanism within this organization that could be used to get this guy out. So why aren't you supporting these complaints?"

blocks.caption: Gianni Infantino (left) and Donald Trump (right) have been close ever since the 2026 World CupImage: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: World Cup for sale
FIFA's plans to sell 20% of the World Cup's commercial rights to private investors caused widespread outrage when they became public in July.

"Football is not for sale," Micallef told DW. "Yes, football needs investment, but that investment does not mean that football has to sell itself. The FIFA leadership is there … to make sure that football grows and reaches more people, but not to profit from it. Football belongs to us, the fans."

Despite the controversy, Infantino has confirmed he will stand for a fourth term as FIFA president next March. The governing body, which didn't respond to DW's request for comment, has closed ranks around its leader, saying previously that there was a "concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its president."
With no sign of Infantino budging, McGeehan called on the EU to intervene, questioning the ability of sports organizations to regulate themselves.

"I think there are a lot of football supporters who are dreadfully concerned about the way the game is run, but think that there is no way to fix it," McGeehan said. "And of course, there's always a way to fix it, and the way to fix it is politics."
Is FIFA breaking EU competition law?
FIFA's role as both competition organizer and football's global regulator has long raised concerns about a conflict of interest.

It is already the subject of a complaint to the European Commission's competition watchdog over its control over the international match calendar. The complaint, filed by the umbrella group representing Europe's domestic football leagues, alleges FIFA abuses its role to favor its own competitions. On Tuesday, the complaint was widened to include the women's game.
Micallef, meanwhile, did not rule out further action.

"The fact that sport is autonomous does not absolve it of its responsibilities under the law," he said. "So I don't exclude competition policy. Competition policy is a tool in our war chest, but I would much rather prefer to address these issues through dialogue than through competition lawyers."
Pointing to the EU's role last year in opposing Spanish and Italian league matches being played outside Europe — proposals heavily criticized by fan groups — Micallef expressed hope for change.

"The football community should never be underestimated. When those who are passionate about football and institutions come together and send a strong message, then we are a power to be reckoned with," said Micallef. "We deserve proper governance. That's not too much to ask."
Matt Pearson contributed reporting to this article.

articles.title: 3 suspects in Degamo slay found guilty of illegal possession of gun, bombs
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—A Manila court has found three former Army soldiers, who were earlier linked to the killing of former Negros Oriental Governor Roel Degamo, guilty of illegal possession of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—A Manila court has found three former Army soldiers, who were earlier linked to the killing of former Negros Oriental Governor Roel Degamo, guilty of illegal possession of firearms and explosives.
Manila Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 40, in an Aug. 18 decision, convicted Joric Labrador of unlawful possession of a firearm and ammunition.
It also found Joven Javier and Benjie Rodriguez guilty of one count each of unlawful possession of explosives in connection with the assassination of Degamo in March 2023.
Labrador was sentenced to up to 10 years in prison, while Javier and Rodriguez were meted a prison term of reclusion perpetua or 20 years.

The court also directed that the firearm and explosives seized from the three accused be handed over to the Philippine National Police.These items include a .45 caliber pistol, two magazines, 14 rounds of live ammunition, and two hand grenades,
The three respondents are also facing multiple murder and frustrated murder and attempted murder charges before the Manila RTC for the killing of Degamo.
The 56-year-old governor was shot down inside his home in Pamploma town, Negros Oriental.
According to the Department of Justice, which brought the charges to the Manila RTC, the validity of warrantless arrests was upheld in these cases.
This is because the confiscated items were properly identified and handled, based on testimonies by the police and other witnesses. /apl

articles.title: DPWH chief Dizon to testify in graft trial of Zaldy Co, others
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon will testify in the trial of former lawmaker Zaldy Co and his co-accused on graft charges in connection with alleged anomalous…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon will testify in the trial of former lawmaker Zaldy Co and his co-accused on graft charges in connection with alleged anomalous flood control project in Mindoro, the Sandiganbayan said on Wednesday.

Associate Justice Maryann Corpuz-Mañalac made this announcement as the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division heard testimonies from two cashier officers of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in Mimaropa (Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon, and Palawan).
“As agreed upon, let the presentation of the next witness in the person of Secretary Vince Dizon proceed on September 23, at 8:30 in the morning,” Corpuz-Mañalac.
Corpuz-Mañalac also said the next witness’ judicial affidavit has been submitted online to the court.

In November 2025, the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division issued arrest warrants against Co and his co-accused from the DPWH and Sunwest Corporation in connection with a P289.9 million road dike project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro, which was flagged as substandard and found to have structural deficiencies.
Co was linked to Sunwest Corporation, which was among the top 15 contractors awarded with the most flood control projects worth P100 billion from July 2022 to May 2025. /gsg

articles.title: NPA leader killed in clash with Army troops in Leyte
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY- A ranking New People’s Army (NPA) leader was killed in a brief clash with government troops on Tuesday afternoon in the hinterlands of Barangay Caridad, Baybay City, Leyte, the…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY- A ranking New People’s Army (NPA) leader was killed in a brief clash with government troops on Tuesday afternoon in the hinterlands of Barangay Caridad, Baybay City, Leyte, the military reported.

The Army’s 8th Infantry Division(ID), which is based in Catbalogan City, Samar, said the encounter occurred on Sept. 8 after soldiers received information from a resident about the presence of armed men allegedly collecting money and food from communities in the area.
Troops from the 802nd Infantry Brigade(IB) proceeded to the area to verify the report, resulting in a firefight that lasted about five minutes, according to the military.
Killed was Erwin Murillo Maceda, alias “Romnick,” who was identified by the Army as the vice team leader of the NPA’s Island Committee Levox under the Eastern Visayas Regional Party Committee.
An M16 rifle was also recovered from the encounter site, the 8th ID said.

Brig. Gen. Pompeyo Jason Almagro, commander of the 802nd IB, said Maceda and his group had allegedly been involved in extortion, threats against residents and business owners, and attacks on government security installations in Leyte.

“The people of Leyte have endured years of fear, intimidation, and disruption caused by armed groups. We will not allow these conditions to return to communities that have worked hard to achieve peace,” Almagro said in a statement released on Wednesday.

The military said the encounter followed reports of armed NPA members attempting to regain their presence in communities where government authorities have declared stable peace and security conditions.
The Army also credited residents’ cooperation and timely reporting for enabling government forces to respond to the reported presence of armed men.
“The cooperation of our communities is critical. Their timely reporting allows government forces to respond before threats can escalate,” Almagro said.
The 8th ID renewed its call for remaining NPA members to abandon armed struggle and surrender, saying government programs are available to assist former rebels who return to civilian life.
The military said it would continue operations in areas where armed groups are reported to be operating while encouraging NPA members to return peacefully to their families and communities./coa

articles.title: INQToday: Romualdez ordered to appear in court, Panelo joins VP’s team
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Here are INQToday’s top stories this afternoon: Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez has been ordered to appear before the Sandiganbayan on September 10 as the anti-graft…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Here are INQToday’s top stories this afternoon:Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez has been ordered to appear before the Sandiganbayan on September 10 as the anti-graft court hears his plea to remain hospitalized while facing a non-bailable plunder case.
